speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SHIPMENT OF SYRUPS FROM WEST INDIES.
speechtext:
I wish to cal) the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the fact that merchants in Quebec doing business with the West Indies have written to me that they cannot get space for molasses and products of that kind on board the subsidized steamers plying between the West Indies and St. John. Their correspondents in the West Indies

tell them that these steamers refuse to take syrups, the whole of the space being taken up by sugar, which, they say, is more paying freight. These merchants say that for some months past they have not been able to obtain any molasses. In view of the fact that these steamers are subsidized by the Government, this matter ought to be inquired into. I would ask the good offices of the Minister of Marine, or of the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he were here, to look into the matter and tell me what answer I may give to my correspondent in Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: SHIPMENT OF SYRUPS FROM WEST INDIES.
speechtext: I shall be very glad to do so, although the matter is one that comes more within the jurisdiction of the Department of Commerce which controls questions of subsidies to .steamboats. I understand that these West Indian steamers during the present winter have been carrying very large cargoes. Although they are much larger boats than were on the route a few years ago, the development of business this winter has been so great that they have been unable to carry all the cargo offered. I presume it is necessary for them to bring the sugar to Canada for the purpose of affording work to the employees of the sugar refineries. I understand from the Minister of Railways that an attempt is now being made to relieve the situation, and it is probable that a boat belonging to the Railway Department, the Durley Chine, may be sent to the West Indies to help relieve the congestion. I shall be glad to make inquiry and to communicate such information as I may obtain to my right hon. friend.

I rise in order to make a personal explanation. In the course of the debate the other evening, I used this language :
And when he suggests there was an alternative proposition from the other side of the House in amendment to the Government measure, he conveniently forgets that the amendment proposed to postpone any action whatever until after a general election should he held in Canada.
Mr. Pugsley: I do not think I proposed that, nor that any one else proposed it.
Sir Robert Borden : Does not the hon. member remember the terms of the amendment?
Mr. Pugsley:	I do not think that was in It.
Sir Robert Borden : He may not think so, but that does not alter the fact that it was in it. His memory is not so good on this as on some other points. I have a distinct recollection that the proposals offered by hon. gentlemen opposite involved the postponement of action until after the general election.
My bon. friend from Pietou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald), at a later stage in the debate, expressed surprise that I should have made th'e statement to which I have alluded; and he read the amendment which was offered by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) on the 12th day of December. I should like to say, in explanation and support of my assertion, that on the I3th of February, 1913, as reported at page 3103 of Hansard, the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) moved a sub-amendment in these words:
That the following words be added at the end thereof:	" and the consent of Parliament
should not he given to this resolution until it
has been submitted to and received the approval of the electors."
That amendment was undoubtedly accepted by my hon. friends on the other side of the House because when it was voted upon on the 13th of February, as is recorded at page 3239 of Hansard, the right hon. leader of the Opposition and all his supporters either voted for or were paired in favour of that sub-amendment. Then, at a later date, on the 18th day of February, as reported at page 3482 of Hansard, 1913, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), upon the second reading of the Bill, moved the following amendment:
That the said Bill be not now read a second time, but that it be resolved:
That it is the constitutional duty of the Government, under the terms of the British North America Act, Immediately to introduce a measure for the readjustment of the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons, according to the population of the said provinces as established by the census of 1911, and that this House do not proceed further with the Bill until such readjustment has taken place, .and the people have been duly consulted on the said Bill.
The leader of the Opposition and his followers voted also for that amendment. To give a perfectly correct statement of the record, I should, in fairness, say that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition and those who supported him voted al^o for the resolution proposed by my hon. friend on the 12th day of December, although they had previously voted for the amendment of the hon. member for Assiniboia. It is an absolute fact that they voted for the sub-amendment and for the amendment on the same day, the one proposing to postpone any action until after the people had been consulted and the other proposing immediate action. Hon. gentlemen on the other side supported by their votes both these propositions. And then, further, I find also that when the Bill reached the Senate, Sir George Ross, the Liberal leader in the Senate, moved the following amendment, which was carried by a vote of 51 to 27:
This Hous? is not justified in giving its assent to this Bill until it is submitted to the judgment of the people.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The policy of my right hon. friend succeeded very well, because his amendment carried in the Senate and the Bill was defeated on that ground. I am giving it as an illustration of the proposals to which I alluded in my reply to the hon. member for St. John.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are you taking up the amended resolutions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I propose that we take up the resolutions relating to the tariff, namely the duty upon apples and upon fuel oil. Tariff item 92, which it is proposed to strike out, provides a tariff of 25 cents, British preferential tariff; 35 cents intermediate tariff, and 40 cents general tariff per barrel of apples. There has also been a special customs tariff under the War Revenue Act of 1915 which amounts to 5 
per cent British preferential; and 74 per cent each in the intermediate and general tariff; that is an ad valorem duty. The new rate is 60 cents per barrel, British preferential, and 90 cents in the intermediate and general tariffs.

Before this duty passes, I would like to say a word or two. I have not troubled my hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) much this year. An unrepentant free trader could not pretend to be altogether dissatisfied with a Budget in regard to which the Minister of Finance and the financial critic of the Opposition are contending with one another as to the best form of direct taxation to impose. That is

a condition of affairs which is eminently satisfactory to one who has been preaching that doctrine in this House for many years. But I do not know why the Minister of Finance, when he was making so courageous and so noble a departure, from my point of view, should not have made it whole-heartedly. Nobody knows better than he that he should not have introduced this duty on apples. He told us last year that the customs tariff was the mainstay of the Finance Minister in the course of twelve months he has managed either to lose or to break his mainstay pretty badly. I wish he had thrown the old thing away altogether, and not bothered the people of the prairie with this trifling miserable little duty on apples. I do not know why he did it; perhaps he will favour me personally with the information. It is a very miserable' little duty, Mr. Chairman, in a Budget that has many good points about it, and it is such a splendid concrete example of the general evils of protection that I feel I am entitled to take up the time of the committee for a minute or two about it.
Speaking on another subject the other day, the Minister of Finance said he was inclined to look at free wheat from the national standpoint. That was a very good sentiment coming from the Minister of Finance of a party who on tariff matters profess always to hold a policy which they call national. How can he defend this tariff on apples from the point of view of a national policy? He did not attempt to do so. The Minister, in his Budget statement, said this is done specifically to help a given industry in a certain province, so that, so far from having anything national about it, it bears the earmark of class, provincialism, or any other word that constitutes narrowness and opposition to what is. in the national interest. It sets the province of British Columbia, if my hon. friend likes to look at it in that way, against the Prairie Provinces; and coming from the Prairie Provinces I should not be true to the best interests of the nation, which are represented very largely in those provinces, if I did not make an emphatic protest to my hon. friend. Why should he put another burden on the Prairie Provinces this year? What have they done? I know that two of the provinces are very Liberal in their complexion, but surely that would never actuate my hon. friend. I know something else about all the Prairie Provinces; 1 know that the people inhabit a part of Canada which perhaps needs fruit more
than any other part of the Dominion. They suffer from the cold climate' of Canada's winter in such a way that fruit is an absolute necessity of their existence, and very essential to theiT health and to their prosperity. Does my hon. friend say he is helping the nation in hurting the health of the sturdy farmers who have given you a crop this year upon which the prosperity of the whole nation depends? I am very much in earnest about this thing, and I hope my hon. friend will listen to me, because I think that before I have finished I shall have pretty nearly moved his distaff or mainstay or whatever he calls it. My hon. friend is a good-hearted man; I know that. He cannot have any internal spite against the people of the prairies. But does he ever think seriatim of the things he has done and is doing to those people? He took an hour and forty minutes to speak against their being allowed to sell their wheat where they want to sell it; and last year he put on a tariff that fell very largely upon those people. Now he comes along, and, after doing his best to prevent them from making money by selling their wheat, he tries to take a portion of the little money they do get for the apple growers of British Columbia. Is it fair or decent to the people of those provinces? I recall to my hon. friend's attention a statement in which we have the true national outlook of a man of vast financial responsibility, who understands this country very well, and who represents West Toronto. At the beginning of last year he said: " Everything in Canada this year depends upon this year's crop." Yet, when Canada depends so much upon those men on the prairies, why should these successive burdens be placed upon them? Pharoah was not in it for a cruel heart with my hon. friend. He set the Israelites to make bricks without straw, but my hon. friend wants the prairie farmers to pay high rates for their apples without selling their wheat. He is a modern Pharoah, and I am ashamed of him, much as I think of him in a great many ways, as I may tell him before I sit down. There is no end to the injustice he is going to mete out to the people of the prairies if I do not get him checked in some way or another. It is a positive sin against the health of the people, and nobody can say that a sin against the health of the people is a very good feature of a national policy. There is nothing national about it; it is very local indeed. It is much more local even than setting up British Columbia against the prairie provinces. It is much worse than
