that because the great majority of the people of British Columbia are not apple producers; they are apple consumers. 'The people of Vancouver do not grow any apples, not at all events on the streets that I saw when I was there. You have 100,000 people in Vancouver who are consumers of apples, so that my hon. friend, in pursuance of this broad national policy that he has produced, is not only setting a portion of British Columbia against the Prairie Provinces, but he is putting a very small portion of British Columbia against the rest of the province. I would like my hon. friend either to give up this or give up professing that he is following the National Policy in tariff changes. The people of Vancouver and Victoria are just as important as the people who produce apples. In regard to the prairies, we find our market for beef to some extent in British 'Columbia, but we in Alberta do not ask my hon. friend to protect us in the raising of beef. We should be ashamed to do it. I do not care where you bring beef from to compete with the steers that we are raising in Alberta, they would never be looked at, they would never get across the line. But why should my hon. friend penalize the men who are raising beef in Alberta? Our beef speaks for itself; why does he not make his apple producing friends produce fruit that would speak for itself?
I have no objection to the men who raise apples, but I have an objection to their economic policy, and I want to point out to my hon. friend that in helping this industry he is following a very false line of economic policy. Does he not know-I am sure lie does, because his knowledge is encyclopaedic that these gentlemen whom he now seeks to protect paid far too much for their land in British 'Columbia? He is going to help out these people with their dear lands. A great many of them are not apple growers at all; lam sorry to say it, but in British 'Columbia there are a great many of my own fellow countrymen, and there is nobody so keen to take advantage of another Englishman as an Englishman who has been in the country for two or three years and who is holding land until he can get some other Englishman to come out and give him more than he paid for it himself. I would be sorry to say that about the apple growers of British Columbia as a whole. All I want them to do is to raise apples on the same principle that we raise beef in Alberta,and that the grain farmers raise wheat in the other provinces.

I remember that the Minister of Trade and Commerce last year, when tariff taxes were being objected to as bearing too heavily upon the farmers of the West, said that he felt quite sure that the farmers of the West would bear , their proper share of the war expenses. I wonder if I could not place similar confidence in thh raisers of apples, because there are two sides to the loyalty business. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was appealing to the farmers of the plains very broadly, and indirectly, and he was putting it in a very complimentary fashion when he sai : I am quite sure that the farmers are such good, patriots that they will stand by these impositions for the sake of the Empire and pay them gladly. But that has two sides to it. Some people's loyalty consists in asking the other fellow to pay, and that is the kind of loyalty I do not believe very much in. I do not think there is much loyalty on the part of those men who raise apples and, who say to me that I have to be loyal enough to pay them more for their apples in time of war than I pay in time of peace. I have not much use for the loyalty that consists mainly in putting such a sacrifice on other people.
Talking of one portion of British Columbia being supported at the expense of the great consuming portions of that province brings me to make an inquiry that I would much rather not have to make. I have always had the very greatest regard for my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. He knows it; his psychology has been a continual and interesting study to me, and there is not a man who has taken more pleasure in observing that the Crown very rightly, as I think, has recognized his very great abilities by giving him a well-earned knighthood. I have the highest appreciation of my hon. friend, and I was delighted when this honour was paid him. We have all been pleased to see the rapidity with which he has fallen into the ways of this House, and the certainty with which he has advanced in the ranks of statesmanship after having been picked up just a little precariously at the last election. Having this great regard, for him, I am just a little sorry that he should have stooped to this miserable piece of politics, or tariff legislation-economics he rather likes to call it. I would suppose he would like to pass it off as good economics, but if he is going te do that I wish he would tell me what he is going to get 'from it because the farmers of the plains will want tp know what revenue he is getting from it. If the

revenue does not justify it, he will have difficulty in justifying it on the ground that he is going to help these men who have given far too much for their land. I am not at all sure that my hon. friend was not actuated hy a motive that I would rather he should not have been influenced .by in introducing this legislation. I am not at all sure that he was so much concerned about the troubles of the apple growers when he introduced this legislation as he was about the troubles in the local administration of British Columbia. I am very suspicious upon that point. If that was his motive, I am bound to say that the charge of shortsightedness which I brought against some of his tariff legislation last year has much more justification even in regard to this legislation because in regard to this he has been extraordinarily shortsighted. He did not see that Victoria and Vancouver people could not possibly take any interest in the raising of the prices oi apples except to resist it. He should have seen it 'because these were places where his apple tariff was going to have the very first chance of producing political effects. They produced effects beyond anything which was looked for by the hon. gentleman. But my hon. friend confusing his economics in that way, I cannot help saying that I can hardly be sorry for him. What he wants to recognize in dealing with economic questions is that they must be put upon a broad principle and the broad principle in regard to production in Canada is that it is not necessary to produce apples at all. What is necessary is that we should eat them. There is nothing in producing apples. My hon. friend, on general principles, goes too far in regard to production. Production is not the great thing that we want in this country; consumption is the great thing. If you undertake to consume plenty you will produce plenty. A -man who does not produce anything gets no wages and his consumption is pretty low. If you look after the consumption of a thing you will never need to be afraid of the production. Consume plenty and production will go on. That is the principle that my hon friend should have gone upon. He has a great sense of humour. If he had not had this sense of humour he would have rejected this course as suicidal because he would never have gone into this thing at al'l for the purpose of restoring the falling fortunes of Sir Richard McBride. We have read in our Shakespeare of another Richard exclaiming
under rather hard stress of circumstances: A horse, a horse; my kingdom for a horse. That Richard, unfortunately, did not get a horse. This Richard did not get a horse but he got a ship and fled from the scene. My hon. friend 'comes to his rescue a little late and says: There is a little duty on apples for you. I do not think it will do much for Mr. Bowser either.
I want to warn my hon. friend solemnly against ward-heeling economics of that kind, for the future of his reputation as Finance Minister of this country. This duty was a paltry miserable duty to bring in at this time, and one which cannot be justified on any sound ground whatsoever. In another speech the other day my hon. friend said that he and the rest of us were looking forward to different things after the war. I am quite sure things will be different, but I do not think that on this question of tariff and economics, things will be different in the sense in which my hon. friend is looking for them to be different. War is the greatest of human re-actions; this is the greatest of all wars; and I personally would die of despair if I did not think that the rebound of the wave towards progress will be the greatest the world has ever seen. And progress is not achieved by going further along the lines of tariff legislation. I cannot help thinking that Providence has taken a very apt pupil in hand in my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, and he took him and the rest of us in hand in rather a vigorous manner when he burned down the old Parliament building. He sent the Minister of Finance down to the Museum here for a special purpose, I am quite sure; and the special purpose I would commend to him is that he should look for progress after the war, and he could not help that progress in any better why than by finding the fossil remains in this building, and putting as much tariff in that part of the building as he possibly can, and leaving it there when he and the rest of us are spared leave here for the new Parliament building. Meanwhile, I would not wait till we make the shift, but I would advise him to find out where the fossil remains are and put this little apple duty among them before it ever has an existence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) has been so complimentary in his remarks towards myself that he disarms antagonism, even political antagonism. He and I are good friends, and I know we should con-

tinue to be so. My hon. friend has spoken of fossils, and it is curious that while he was speaking I should have been thinking of our being housed in this museum. I was throwing my mind forward to the period after the war in which, along with the other changes that will have taken place, my hon. friend from Red Deer will either have reformed or be one of the few remaining free-traders, in which latter case the museum might be an appropriate place to house him as a specimen of an extinct race of economists. All that is quite within the limits of the possibilities of this war. The trouble with my hon. friend is that he got started wrong; he was caught young, and he has never got over it. He can see no good whatever in protection. Well, I look forward to the conversion of my hon. friend. He has spoken of himself as an unrepentant sinner, but some of the greatest sinners in the world have been converted.
I said an unrepentant free-trader.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And the conversion of a hardened sinner is usually sudden and frequently lasting. I recall the case of John Bunyan, and of Saul of Tarsus, who was converted when a great light suddenly burst on him on his way to Damascus. When this war is over and my hon. friend sees what free trade has meant as between Great Britain and Germany, and realizes the advantages of a self-contained country and a self-contained Empire, I should not be surprised if almost as great a light bursts on him as fell on Saul of Tarsus on his way to Damascus. And I look forward to most eloquent speeches from him, in this House, if he should be here, in favour of protection as the true economic policy of this country.
My hon. friend has spoken of the National Policy, and has asked what relation this duty on apples has to the National Policy. Well, it seems to me that the basic and most important industry in Canada to-day is agriculture. A part of agriculture is the growing of apples, and it does seem to me that it would be a most desirable thing if Canada should, as she undoubtedly can, not only raise all the apples required for the people of this country, but have a large surplus over for export. There is no reason in the world why Canada should not raise all the apples consumed in this country. It is simply a matter of distribution.

Before I come to the matter in hand, my hon. friend from Red Deer repeated a remark I made last year, that the tariff was the mainstay of revenue. That is quite correct. I should like to see my hon. friend as Minister of Finance endeavouring by any other means to provide the amount of money that we require to meet our expenditures and increased interest charges due to this war.
Is the proposed increase in the duty on apples for the purpose of revenue or to protect the farmers of British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As stated in my remarks on the Budget, this duty is in my view indispensably necessary for the safeguarding of the apple industry of Canada, and particularly of British Columbia. It is frankly for that purpose. My hon. friend spoke of loyalty, and he was rather unhappy in his remarks because it chances that no district in Canada has evinced its loyalty in more striking fashion than the fruit growing district of British Columbia.

Is my hon. friend quite fair? I was talking purely of loyalty to taxation. The last remark I would wish to make is that one section of the country is giving more soldiers than another; we had better leave that out. My hon. friend will admit that I have never indulged in talk of that kind at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend did not make it quite clear in his remarks to what he was referring when he spoke of loyalty. However, I accept his explanation.
Coming to the matter in hand, there is a very extraordinary situation in British Columbia. I deprecate very much the references made by one or two hon gentlemen opposite to the British Columbia political situation, a question to which this duty on apples has absolutely no relationship whatever. The question of raising the duty on apples has been before my department for not less than three years. Every year there have been deputations, and the fruit-growers of British Columbia have made the strongest kind of representations as to the serious situation that exists there, and have asked for some kind of relief. So no question possibly arises as to this duty on apples being connected with the British Columbia political situation. The Government have acted with no haste in the matter. Representations have been made to us for the last two or three years, and we finally came to the conclusion that unless some kind of tariff were granted-
What were the representations made by the delegations from British Columbia in regard to the apple industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The British Columbia fruit grower is in competition with an abnormal condition of affairs that exists in the states of Washington, Oregon and Idaho. In these states there has been a very great over-production, and my hon. friend, knows that, with the planting that has been going on for the last few years, over-production is likely to greatly increase in the future. The fact of the matter is that apples produced in these states have been selling on the American side as well as in Canada at much less than the cost of production.
What is the quantity *bf~British Columbia's export of apples in carloads?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Is it not true of every apple-growing country that many apples are sold at less than the cost of production?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may be true. But in British Columbia this has been a standing condition for a considerable time past, and such a condition has been reached that unless this tariff measure is granted the consequence for the British Columbia fruit-growing industry will be most serious. Apart from British Columbia, it is to be remembered that two years ago we had in-Canada a condition in which it was almost impossible to dispose of the apple crop. It looked as if apples were to be left to rot under the trees. The Minister of Trade and Commerce embarked upon a campaign and assisted in relieving the situation. All the signs point to a large increase in the apple crop for this year, and^ for that matter, for many years to come, op account largely of the extensive planting that has taken place in Tecent years. It comes down to this: Is there any reason why the Canadian fruit grower-not confining the argument to British Columbia, but taking the ifruit industry from the Atlantic to the Pacific-should not be given the benfit of the Canadian market? It does not necessarily mean that the price of this fruit will go up; it means that the Canadian grower will have a better opportunity in his own market, and that, I believe, is the true national policy.
What is the good of it if it will not put the price up?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then the hon. gentleman's argument is that no matter how high the tariff may be, even if prohibitive, foreign goods will still come in3
Not necessarily.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My argument is, that with this increase in the duty, the Canadian market will be reserved more for the Canadian grower. It does not necessarily mean-

The hon. gentleman
is getting away from the point, and I want to hold him to it. He tells us that the British Columbia apple producer is engaged in a losing industry because he cannot obtain a price which will yield him a profit. The hon. gentleman proposes to improve that condition by increasing the duty. But how will the increase in the duty improve the situation, unless it enables the producer to get a bigger price. And how can he get a bigger price unless he gets it from the Canadian producer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The greater
market for his product in Canada.

Mr. MAC'LBAN: We only imported 269,000 barrels of apples last year in all Canada; that would not help very much.
Sir 'THOMAS WHITE: The British Columbia fruit-growing district is not a very large one, but it is a very important and growing section in British Columbia, and the effect of this, we hope, will be to give them a larger market in Canada for their product.
What does their yearly production amount to?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The British Columbia yield in boxes has been as follows:
Boxes.
1910		 210,000
1911		 250,000
1912		 430,000
1913		 477,000
1914		 685,000
1915		 787,750
My hon. friend will observe that the production in 1915 was nearly four times as much as in 1910.

Were they not doing
well enough?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, they were not doing well enough; they have not been doing well at all. As I say, unless this tariff change is introduced, the future of the British Columbia fruit-growing industry is of a most precarious character. I do not believe that any hon. gentleman would like to see an important section of the community most seriously affected by a condition of affairs that can be remedied by legislative action in this House, and such action not taken.

There might be
some other way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would be glad to have suggestions as to a way. 1 do not know of any other way to assist the situation.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce ('Sir George Foster) promised a couple of years ago to find a market in Australia.
The position of affairs, as I understand it, is one of only this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

I thought the first excuse given was that the condition of affairs is serious because of the great over-produc-

tion in the United States. But the minister says that that is' not correct, that this is a permanent tariff that he hopes to have remain as long as he is in power. He says that is correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I make no statement as to how long a tariff condition will continue; it would be most improper to do so.

Rightly or wrongly I
had the impression, either from what was said in the Budget or from some other reliable source, that it was on account of the condition of affairs this year-a great overproduction in Washington, Oregon and Idaho-that this action was necessary. If I am incorrect in that-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has been for the last three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Was there any tariff on apples during the tenure of office of tire late Government, of which imy hon. friend was so ardent a supporter? If so. what does my hon. friend say about that?
I am afraid there was a tariff.
Oh, oh.

Since the minister has
raised that point, I may say what I said in this House eight or ten years ago; I support the Liberal party not because of their tariff, but in spite of it. There is nothing on which my mind is clearer than on this point: in the interests of my people, in the interests of the Dominion of Canada, as between the two parties in this country I shall continue to support the Liberal party.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Did not my hon. friend, when in opposition support a tariff policy? Did he not frequently say from his place in Parliament that a tariff policy was right?
I do not recollect that.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: What about farm implements?

I repeat that as between the two parties I would not do anything to put the high protection party in power, and to put the Liberal moderate tariff party out. But if there were a real, genuine free trade party in this House, I would have to support that free trade policy. No person by any political knavery or fakirism or anything of that kind, can convince mo that I ought to support the greater of two evils- because I look on tariffs altogether as an evil. I am just as clear on this point before my constituents as I am in [DOT]this House. The people of the Prairie Provinces would be very foolish if of the two parties they did not support the Liberal party at this juncture. Let us take this case as a case in point. It is not a large matter; it is a little measly matter, as measly as some of the apples that come from British Columbia. This duty on apples is the thin end of the wedge. Hon. gentlemen opposite want to see how the people of the Prairie
Provinces will stand a little touching up along the line of duties. Perhaps another tariff commission will be suggested to us before long. In his speech the other day *the Solicitor General said: "How could we give you an open market for wheat? If we give you an open market, the *first	thing	we	know you	will	wantfree	trade	in	something	else; one
thing will lead to another, and it may come to the point that the protection business will be knocked on the head." The hen. gentleman said in effect: "We cannot give you an open market, because if you get a taste for it, you will be anxious for more." The hon. gentleman did not use these w'ords, but that is what he meant. This matter of a duty on apples is not a *large matter, but it is all the meaner and all the more unfortunate that this miserable, measly, picayune, small business should come from the Minister of Finance at a time when people ought to be great and big in financial matters. I do not think any one cares a great deal about the money part of it, because the amount involved is not very large; it is the principle of the thing that we object to. Why put it all on the people of Saskatchewan and Alberta? If you want to encourage the apple growing industry, why not do so by providing better storage facilities? Why not assist the industry at the expense of the federal treasury? Surely hon. gentlemen could do something that would make it advantageous for our people to buy British Columbia apples. Surely the brains of the Government could devise some means by which the industry could be encouraged if hon. gentlemen want to encourage it. I think there is a great deal in what the hon. member for Red Deer said: that a great deal of the trouble comes from the fact that these lands in British Columbia are held at such outrageously high prices. The Creator intended that these lumber fields and fruit gardens should be used by the people, but they have got into the hands of speculators Favourites of the McBride Government got them as pap, and they have so shuffled them that a grant of land which they got for practically nothing, after changing hands a few times, was worth millions of dollars. Then the people of the Prairie Provinces are told: You have got to pay a price for your lumber which will pay interest on the absurd capitalization of the timber limits; you must pay a price on your fruit which will cover the interest on the absurd capitalization of the British Columbia fruit fields. The minig-

ter has remarked that this duty will not increase the cost of apples. Even after having been subject to the sobering influence of the last year or so since the war commenced, the minister could not help laughing when he made that statement. To say that it will not make higher prices to the apple growers is a joke-a pretty serious joke, because of the principle that is involved in it. The Minister of Finance is a great statesman in some respects, but even great statesmen sometimes make childish statements, and I think the statement thai this duty will not mean larger prices to the people who raise apples is one which is unworthy of the man who fills the position of Finance Minister of Canada. I hope that the minister will rise in his place and withdraw that statement.

I have followed
this discussion so far with considerable interest and some amusement. One would almost infer from the remarks which have been made with regard to the proposed duty on. apples that Canada was a rather small country in which apple growing was confined to a very small area, and that this duty is really going to affect only the people of the prairie provinces. I protest against any assertion of that kind. I would like to remind the House that this duty has been asked for, not only by the people of British Cotanbia, but by the people of other provinces as well.

May I point
out that the hon. minister, in his Budget speech, said the exact opposite of what my hon. friend says? He used the words "especially British Columbia;" therefore our criticism is directed against the statement of the minister. >

I am dealing with the arguments advanced in committee this afternoon; I trust that the hon. gentleman will grant me the privilege of confining my remarks to those arguments. This has been a very live question in Canada for quite a number of years; the situation has not been more acute during the past year than it was for many years previous. Any one who has followed the fruitgrowing industry in the Dominion of Canada will readily understand that the past year was not the worst year in the history of our country so far as the importation of American fruit is concerned.
But we do know that there is in the United States a combine among the wholesale

fruit dealers which practically forces the retailers in' Canada to take so much of the American apples and similar fruit, that we can very well grow in this country, whether they went to or not, if they are to receive a supply of such fruit as oranges which we do not produce. It is nothing new to the people of this country to see the fruit stores in our large cities at this time of the year practically filled with fruits from the western United States, Oregon, and Washington territory. The importations in the last five years have been very large. In 1911, they were 150,000 barrels; in 1912,
195,000	barrels; in 1913, 320,000 barrels; in 1914, 331,700 barrels, and in 1915, 269,01X1 barrels. Thus we did not suffer so very much from American importations in the past year as in the two previous years. British Columbia undoubtedly has great prospects, there is a great future in store for it as a fruit producing country; but in the province of Ontario there are even greater posibilities for the growing of fruit than in any other province. These possibilities have been overlooked, but we find at present there is at least $50,000,000 invested in apple orchards in Ontario, which is more than double the amount in any other province. This question is quite a live issue in Ontario. If we are ever going to make of Canada a great nation, we have got to give and take a little among ourselves. Some parts of Canada may not be adapted to a certain industry while other parts are, and if we are going to build up and develop these parts that possibly have advantages, then we must suitably regulate our tariff. The hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) could not but hark back to the wheat question this afternoon, and it is only a few days since I heard hon. gentlemen opposite admit that the wheat from western Canada commands from 7 to 8 cents more on the Liverpool market by reason of the fact that it retains its own identity. That is surely something to be proud of. If you attend the meetings of the apple-growers associations in the city of Chicago, where they have the greatest exhibit of fruit that is to be found in the world, you will invariably find that the quality of the apples grown in Canada is better than that of those grown in the United States.
Then why so much duty?

It is true that the American apple has a better appearance. The apples grown in Oregon and Washington territory, with their d,ry climate, develop a beautiful colour; they have a wax-

like appearance, but they have not the quality of the Canadian apple. That is evident to every one. A few years ago, when the Festival of Empire exhibition was going on in London, the apples selected for exhibition by the Department of Agriculture of Canada were not grown in Britisli Columbia, or in the Annapolis valley, but in a section of Ontario that a few years ago was shown on the map as being outside of the apple-growing district, in the inland counties of Western Ontario; the apples which were shown were selected by the Government of hon. gentlemen opposite from apples grown in the county of Oxford, from which I come. The apple growing industry in Canada is practically in its infancy, and under proper conditions there are great possibilities for its development. It will frequently be found that the Americans are dumping their surplus stock into Canada at times when, in order to keep up the market at home, they can afford to dispose of their surplus in this country at a low rate to the injury of our fruit growers. If you are going to have a stable industry you cannot permit it to be subjected to competition of that kind, and I say the Government are entitled to a great deal of credit for having placed this item in the tariff at this time in order to enable that great industry to be developed as it ought to be. It will redound to the credit of this Government in years to come, and I am satisfied the people of Western Canada are not going to suffer as a result of the increase in the tariff. They will be purchasing apples from the people of British Columbia, and of Ontario, and of the Maritime Provinces, and the people in those provinces will .be purchasing from them many things that they will be able to raise; a reciprocal trade will be carried - on between the various provinces, which will be much better than a trade carried on with people who are prepared to take every possible advantage in dealing with us. That question was settled, and settled for all time, in 1911. The people of Canada spoke at that time and stated emphatically where they stood with regard to any arrangement of that kind. It is simply a waste of time for us to hark back to anything of that nature to-day because we may as well face the issue fairly and squarely, as I am satisfied for one that if there is any part of Canada that feels there is not a sufficient area in Canada to grow enough fruit for the people of Canada, they are making a great mistake. We are an exporting people as far as apples are concerned.

Nobody would
deny that. There is no necessity of the hon. member making an argument that we can produce sufficient apples for our own consumption, because we do that today and much more; we export. The question is, where are you going to get the market?
Yes, we export today, and so do the Americans, by reason of the conditions that exist, they are prepared to unload their surplus stock on Canada in order to reduce that stock-
Only 200,000 barrels.

It was 269,000 barrels last year, 331,000 the year before, and
320,000	the year before that. This is not a small amount to be coming in each year under those conditions, and when you see in our large cities in Ontario, such as Toronto, that the fruit stores are largely supplied with American apples, then I say there is something wrong and it is time for the Government to take some action with regard to the matter.
Will the hon. gentleman explain just why Canadians buy Oregon apples to-day?

I thought I made
that quite clear, it is not a matter of today but a matter of years.
Is it a matter of price?

Apples have been
sold in Ontario much lower than in United States for years past. Just for the very reason that the Apple Growers' Association in the United States are bound to Bet rid of their surplus stock in some way in order to keep up the prices in their own markets.

The question of national
policy and national preference is no new question in this House. The principle has been in operation for many years past. During that time the various Ministers of Finance who have had tariff matters to regulate have tried from time to time to make the burdens bear equitably upon the whole people of Canada, and at the same time protect certain manufacturers and certain industries that needed protection in this Dominion. When hon. members opposite saw fit to attempt to find in the British Columbia provincial by-elections the reason for the Finance Minister dealing with this question at this particular time, they were very

unfair, and had no knowledge apparently of the facts. Delegation after delegation has come to the Capital city during the last four or five years, not only from British Columbia, but from the other fruit-growing districts in Canada, and have sought to have a duty placed upon apples that would enable them to supply our own markets. At this particular time in the history of the Dominion, a delegation from British Columbia arrived, and again pressed the claims of the apple-growers of Canada upon the attention of the Minister of Finance. They pointed out that, so far as British Columbia was concerned, we were not a manufacturing country. We were being taxed under a tariff for almost everything that we used. The few things that we could supply to the balance of Canada were not in the happy position of being sufficiently protected to enable us to retain that market.	'
The question has been asked this afternoon as to how we are going to keep this market without materially increasing the prices. If we could get the whole of the market of Canada, we would be in a better position to deal directly with the consumer. We would practically have a market for the whole of our product, or the greater portion of it, and we would be able to supply a better class of fruit than we have been supplying in the past. The hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) seemed to be surprised because apple growing in the province of British Columbia had increased from 210,000 boxes in 1910 to 787,750 boxes in 1915. Surely he knows that in British Columbia this industry is practically an infant industry. The increase in production is not because of the prices, and not because of the money that is being made out of the sale of apples, but because the trees are coming into bearing. The apple growers of the Western States, particularly those of Oregon, Washington and Idaho, have planted apples over something like
550,000	acres of land. Their production is so great that 75 per cent of their trees will have to be uprooted, and the acreage put to other purposes; and then when those remaining trees are in full bearing, they will have sufficient to supply their own markets. So far as British Columbia is concerned, we have not as yet any over-production, and we are not likely to have any. The cost of producing a box of apples today is, on the average, about $1.08, and that is not based on any extravagant value for the land. The Fruit Growers Association representatives who were here told me 
that the estimated value of apple growing land was $125 per acre, and any one knows that that is not an exorbitant price for land in the valleys of British Columbia.
The situation at present is that there is such an enormous over-production in the three western states which I have mentioned, that, when the growers there have graded their apples, they make the price on the prairies and sell their lower grades in Canada, they having far more than sufficient of the better grades to supply their ordinary market.

Has the hon. member
any idea as to the price the grower in Washington and Oregon receives for his apples, say for No. 1 Fancy?
Forty cents a box.

It is not 40 cents a box.
Time and time again they have flooded the prairie districts with apples at from 30 to 70 cents per box. Occasionally they get as high as $1 and $1.20 for some of the better grades, but these apples very seldom come into our prairies.
I meant apples comparing with your No. 1 grade.

The better grade do not
come in at all to the Prairie Provinces.
I know differently.

I had occasion to make some remarks about the apple duty when I spoke on the Budget. I want to express the opinion again that I expressed on that occasion, and it is that this increased duty on apples means an increased cost to the consumers on the prairies. I am not relying upon any gift of prophesy which I may possess for that assertion, but I have read a statement made by a Vancouver wholesale fruit merchant, and his statement is that it means an increased cost to the consumer. He presents the usual protection argument, and he says the duty could not have any other effect, and that the more protection there is on fruit the greater will be the price demanded by the distributor.

Is the hon. gentleman aware of the arrangement which is about to be consummated between the large co-operative apple growers of Ontario and British Columbia and the Grain
Growers Associations in the western provinces whereby the Grain Growers Associations will distribute all the apples required by the western country instead of allowing the fruit to be handled by a trust?

During last year the United Farmers of Alberta were distributing apples on that basis. But that does not make any difference practically in regard to the matter and that does not mean that the fruit growers of British Columbia will not take advantage of this increased duty when they will be without competition from Washington and Oregon. They will charge more to the men who distribute the fruit and the price will go up; there is no question about that. The hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Green) argued that deputations have been coming here and pressing this matter upon the Government and that finally the Government has yielded to the argument that they " have put up and granted this increase of duty. I understand that these deputations have been coming for the last three or four years. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) dealt with the political side of this assistance to the fruit growers. An expression frequently used by the hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) is that certain things synchronize with certain other things, and if that be true is it not peculiar that this year, when there is a possibility of an election in British Columbia and when there are by-elections in that province, this Government grants this request and gives the apple growers this increased duty. The argument of my hon. friend from Red Deer holds absolutely good on that question. The request is complied with in 1916 when the life of the British Columbia Legislature is expiring.
Another point. Deputations have been coming to this Government, since it cams into power in 1911, from the grain growers of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba asking for free wheat, and their requests have not been complied with up to the present. The Finance Minister tells us that he is assuming a national position. The national position he takes is that of a supporter of one industry in this country-the milling industry. While he takes this attitude in connection with free wheat he comes to the assistance of the fruit growers of British Columbia; or at least he says he is coming to their assistance. This means a further increase in the cost of apples to the consumers of the prairies. If the Minister of

Finance had investigated fruit conditions in British Columbia he would have found that there were other reasons than the competition from the states of Oregon and Washington for the condition of that industry. The statement was made in 1911 by a gentleman who was opposed to the reciprocity measure that reciprocity, in so far as it affected the fruit industry, would be a good thing for the fruit growers of British Columbia. His argument was that if they were compelled to feel the effects of real competition from across the line they would box their fruit better and they would go out and hunt for a market and get it. That is about what will happen to the fruit growers of British Columbia. The British Columbia Department of Agriculture carried on an extensive advertising campaign in Alberta last year and there were fine window displays of British Columbia fruit in the stores of my city. I am satisfied that the increase in the sale of British Columbia fruit in Lethbridge amounted to at least fifty per cent. They advertised and appealed to the people to buy British Columbia fruit, they displayed it in the windows and they gave the people some idea of the kind of fruit they were able to produce. That is what they had failed to do in past years. When Alberta has a surplus of butter to sell it does not come to this Government and ask to have an increased duty on butter. It goes to British Columbia and develops a market. It produces a good article and therefore it is able to dispose of its surplus butter. The fruit growers of British Columbia should cultivate a market in the neighbouring provinces and not come to this Parliament for an increased duty to stifle competition and cause an increase in the cost of fruit to the people of the prairies.
The Minister of Finance is interested in the development of Canada. He wants to see imigration into this country, he wants to see the Prairie Provinces, as well as the other provinces, prosper, and he wants to see an inflow of population after the war. My judgment is that as long as people come to Western Canada, investigate the conditions there and find that the cost of living is high and is increasing, he is. going to interfere with immigration by such legislation as this. What will follow in connection with this duty on fruit? The people who come over to Western Canada from the United States are accustomed to getting fruit and getting it fairly cheaply. When they come to the West and find that apples are expensive, when we put an almost pro-

hibitive duty on American apples coming into this country, and when we increase the cost of .apples so that ordinary people will not be in a position to buy them, do we not interfere with people coming and settling on the western prairies?
My hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) says that this duty will help the apple industry in Ontario. All well and good, but it does not help the farmers of Western Canada who have to buy fruit and who have to pay high prices for it. They do not raise fruit to any extent, nor will they do so for many years to come in those provinces. They have to import it from other provinces, and why should they not be in a position to get that fruit at the best possible price? We will buy British Columbia fruit when the fruit raisers produce that fruit, box it and get it to us in good shape as they have been doing during the past year. They have made a step in that direction, they have created a demand and that demand will increase. But I am afraid that if this Parliament increases the duty on apples and puts the fruit growers of British Columbia-if not the fruit growers, the middlemen-in a position to charge an increased price for their apples, it will do a great deal of harm to their present market on the prairies and will consequently do harm to the fruit growers themselves. That statement was made in a paper published in British Columbia which I have read only recently. The statement was made that this duty might interfere with ' the present market of the British Columbia fruit grower on the prairies because the fruit grower might take advantage of the high protection and increase the cost to the consumer. I would like the Minister of Finance to consider seriously the objections which have been made by the Prairie Provinces to this increased duty on apples, especially, as he says it is according to his own statement, for the benefit of only one province.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I said for the
benefit of the whole apple industry but especially that of British Columbia.
I read in the report of the minister's speech a statement that it was particularly for British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I spoke of the
apple industry generally and of that of British Columbia particularly. What is the whole sentence?

I will read it:

We regard this duty as indispensably necessary for the preservation of the apple growing industry of Canada and particularly that of British Columbia, which has been most-seriously affected since the outbreak of the war.
I still contend that this djity is directed principally to the province of British Columbia. I do not think the war h-ae had any effect on the apple industry of that province, except to increase the market for British Columbia apples, in the Prairie Provinces. I am satisfied that there has been an increase in that market during the last year.

Are we to understand that the Grain Growers' Association and the other farmers' associations, who will act as middlemen in distributing amongst the Prairie Provinces the output of the apple industry of British Columbia and Ontario, will charge excessive -prices to the oeople in those Prairie Provinces?

Leave the middlemen out of the question -altogether, and say that the fruit is bought direct from the fruit growers in British Columbia. I am satisfied that the fruit growers will demand a higher price for their product by reason of the fact that under this tariff competition will be got rid of. There is no question about that. These fruit growers are only human, and they will take advantage of this increase in the tariff.
Not necessarily.

I desire to make a few brief observations on this question, and to deal with -one or two points raised by hon. gentlemen -opposite. Taking the last point first, the main objection of hon. gentlemen opposite seems to be that this duty will mean an increased price to the *apple consumers of the Prairie Provinces.
All over Canada.

I am glad my hon. friend has taken in the whole of Canada. That puts the question on a broader and a much better basis. However, I was referring to the statement that had been made by my hon. friend from Red Deer and others that the duty would mean -an increased cost to the consumers of the Prairie Provinces.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. I mentioned particularly the city which he represents in this House.
Of 5 p.m. course, I pointed out that the minister was short-sighted because he could not see that that would be the effect.

My hon. friend dfb not see it.
Air. CLARK.:	The people of Vancouver
saw it.
Aly hon. friend never saw it at all. He tried to make the argument that this was a political measure. As a matter of fact, it is a measure-I am speak-

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
ing of the local and not of the national aspect-to save an industry in British Columbia which at the present time is not over-producing, arid which for the next five years will not produce to the extent of its natural market's demand. It has also been argued that one of the reasons that the apple industry in British Columbia is in hard, straits is because of the nigh price of land. That has not been demonstrated by any figures, or been attempted to be proved by hon. gentlemen opposite. As a matter of fact, it is not the reason at all. In the first place the land in British Columbia upon which the fruit is grown is perfectly useless-I am referring to the Okanagan valley and the Dry Belt

unless it is irri-. gated, and irrigation works demand a large investment of -capital. On-ce this land is irrigated it produces and becomes valuable. But there must be a large and a long investment before the apple industry becomes a paying proposition. It is, perhaps, six, or eight, or nine years before you get a crop off your trees. The trees have to be sprayed and fertilized in this non-productive period; you have to cultivate the land, keep up the fences, and put in irrigation works. All these things enter into the cost of production of apples. In the Western States I have referred to, it can be demonstrated conclusively that they have over-produced. Large areas of land have been planted in apple orchards and other fruit, and the trees are now coming into bearing at a very rapid rate. A very large percentage of these fruit growers are going into liquidation, and the British Columbia fruit grower is faced with the competition of a bankrupt community. Now, that is not a fair competition. My hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) used the butter illustration. As a matter of fact, he and the hon. member for Bed Deer, and others engaged in the butter business, have a protection for their own market.
Apples are protected to ibout 25 per cent.
This will make it about 25 per cent.
This will make it about 100 per cent.

Not at all. This will make the duty about 25 per cent of the actual market value of the apples. That is clear and beyond question. The butter argument is not reasonable. If the farmers in the Western States of the United

States were shipping their butter into Alberta at a lower price than the Alberta farmers could produce butter at, the farmers of Alberta would be down here 1,500 strong, howling for protection.
No.

There is no question about it. And in such a case my hon. friend from Red Deer would be a convert from free trade.
Mr. MoCRANEY: What price does the apple grower get in British Columbia, so that we can compare it with this duty of 90 cents a barrel?
They get about 22 cents a box in the orchard.
And the duty is 13 cents.
My hon. friend (Mr. Douglas) will not argue that 22 cents a box is a reasonable price to the grower. Does he make that argument?

No.
Mr. STEVEN-S: No,-no more than he will make the argument that 30 cents a bushel is a fair price for wheat or 15 cents a pound a fair price for butter. He must grant to- the grower in one department of agriculture what he claims for another. All we ask for the grower is a reasonable price-a living wage, if you like that term.

The hon. gentleman has misinterpreted my meaning. I was trying to get at the relation of this duty to the price. If the grower is selling at 22 cents a box, would not the customs authority be justified in taking that as a basis for duty?

That is the price to the producer, in the orchard. I think the fair price to consider for duty is the wholesale price in the market.
Mr. M-cCRANEY:. At what price can -the fruit grower of British Columbia raise a barrel of apples profitably?
About $1.08 a box for No. 1.
Is that $1.08 per box or per barrel?

Per box. That is for the No. 1 apples. Of course it would be less for the No. 2 grade, or the No. 3 grade which is equal to the "C" grade imported from the United States, which is our keen competitor. Give us a fair chance in the market of Canada, so that we shall be

assured of marketing a reasonable quantity of our crop, and we will be able to sell that apple at a very little increase, if any increase at all, over the cost at the present time. My hon. friend should remember that the chief cost of thfe apple as it comes on the market is transportation and distribution.
Tl}e transportation charges would be in addition to the cost that the hon. gentleman gave a moment ago?

Certainly. The main difficulty in the marketing of apples to-day lies in the cost of distribution. The distribution has been greatly improved within the last few years. I understand from the chairman of the Railway Commission that transportation has been brought down to the lowest possible figure, so that that consideration can be eliminated from the argument. We come down to the wholesaler or commission merchant who handles the freight. This is a perfectly legitimate business, and I have no complaint to make of the men in the business. But it seems to me that in connection with the fruit business, what we require is that the grower should get into direct touch with his market. There is no business which lends itself better to that method of distribution than apple growing, for you have the apples in packages which can be handled and distributed easily. As stated by my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), efforts have been made, and with a measure of success, to bring the grain growers' organization of the Prairie Provinces-a very fine organization-into cooperation with s the western fruit growers, so as to save the cost of distribution. I suggest to my hon. friends who have been putting up this, as I consider it, rather bitter objection to this clause-a very strong objection at least-that they had better facilitate the co-operation between these two great agricultural bodies, whose interests are common, and endeavour to overcome this economic loss or wastage occasioned by distribution. My hon. friend spoke a little while ago about the importations into Vancouver, and 'he expressed the opinion that this legislation would be against the interests of the people of Vancouver which is the chief centre of population in British Columbia. I must thank my hon. friend for his solicitude for the people of Vancouver. On the other hand, I think I know a little about Vancouver, and 1 would 1122
say to him that the people of that city realize that the development of the hinterland of British Columbia is to their advantage. My hon. friend was in Vancouver in 1911, and I listened to him with a great deal of interest in his discussion of the reciprocity proposals. He and his friends pointed out what an immediate advantage reciprocity would be to the people of Vancouver. There may have been some truth in some of these statements, but the people of Vancouver were far-sighted and they realized that their best interest lay in the development of the whole country rather than in the immediate reduction in price of some of their food commodities. I am quite satisfied to go before my constituents on the basis of supporting the development of the agricultural sections of British Columbia, knowing that the development of these sections will tend to benefit the city of Vancouver and other centres of population.
The hon. member for Red Deer pointed out in rather eloquent terms that this was a very reactionary war, that all wars were reactionary and this particularly so.
I did not say that this war was particularly reactionary. I said this was the greatest war in history, and I said that generally war was reactionary.

That seems to me to be splitting hairs. The hon. gentleman said that war was reactionary and that this was the greatest war in history, and the inference is that this is the most reactionary war. But I would point my hon. friend to the action of the people of Manchester -the home of his idol, Richard Co'bden, a man whose memory I also revere and honour-who, the larger majority of them have already declared in favour of a policy of protection.
Surely my hon. friend is not serious. He would not suggest that a majority of the Chamber of Commerce constitute a majority of the inhabitants of a place of three-quarters of a million people.

I presume that the
Chamber of Commerce represents the views of that great commercial city, which was the cradle of free trade, and has been its home at least, since 1841.
From that time until within the last six months they never uttered a word that could lead one to think that they were in the slightest degree departing from the

policy of free trade. They had weeks of debate on this subject, and a majority whicli threatened to be almost overwhelming declared in favour of the policy of protection. Just as sure as the sun will rise to-morrow, a policy of protection within the Empire is coming. I do not apologize for defending a measure of protection.' My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition for fifteen years stood solidly by the policy of protection, and if he came into office to-morrow he would stand solidly by protection again. He dare not go before the country and say that he would not. The hon. member for Red Deer is consistent; so far as I know, he has always stood for free trade. I always admire a consistent man, but I certainly do not agree with the views of the hon. member for Red Deer. I do not think that any member on the other side of the House would go as far as he does in standing by free trade. Views similar to those which he entertains have now been abandoned by the people of Manchester, represented by the Chamber of Commerce, which has been the birthplace, the cradle, the home of free . trade.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is the Manchester attitude that of free trade within the Empire, or protection within the Empire?

They have changed
their whole ideas as to trade; they have abandoned free trade as it has been in England. I would tell the hon. member for Red Deer, the champion of free trade in this country, that to a large extent the preparedness of Germany and her success in prosecuting this war as she has up to the present time have been the result of the policy of free trade in England.
Does my hon. friend refer to Germany's preparedness on sea?
I do.

She has scarcely been
been heard of on sea.

It was not the policy
that my hon. friend advocated in 1912 that made Great Britain prepared on sea. If it had not been for the bull-dog policy of Winston Churchill, in my estimation there would be no Canada to-day. My hon. friends opposite laugh, but I say further, that whatever be our judgment of Winston Churchill's action in connection with the Dardanelles or with other matters, we must admit that the policy which he followed for years before the outbreak of war made

it possible for Great Britain to control the seas as she does, and as she did within twenty-four hours after the outbreak of war.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I feel it my duty to
direct the attention of the committee to the fact that we are discussing a proposed resolution to amend an item in the tariff. I would respectfully suggest that hon. members refrain from discussing the naval issue.	[DOT]

In justification of my
dealing with this subject, I may say that I was simply referring to a suggestion made by the hon. member for Red Deer. I say this to hon. gentlemen from the Prairie Provinces: give us a fair chance to market a larger quantity of our crop, and we will keep down the prices. That is a sound economic argument. If hon. gentlemen will bend their efforts towards encouraging the co-operation of these two branches of agricultural industry, they will do greater service to the country than they can do by fighting this proposed amendment to the tariff.

Will the hon. gentleman
tell the committee what he considers to be a fair average price to the British Columbia grower for average grade apples, delivered in Vancouver?

We do not handle our
apples just as they are handled in my hon. friend's part of the country. We put them up in boxes, and handle them in very carefully selected grades, under severe inspection laws and regulations. The usual grades on the market are the first, second, and third grades.
What price does the wholesale merchant pay for the average grade?
I should judge from 90 cents to $1.75 a box. Of course, I do not speak authoritatively.

The h6n. gentleman says
that this is a measure to save an industry. If that be the case, the consumer pays to that industry an amount sufficient to save it. For one barrel of apples that we import into Canada, we export four. I think it would be found that a very large proportion of the total. importation of 267,000 barrels was brought in between seasons, that is, in the months of May, June and July, from the southern portion of the United States. 1 cannot understand why the producers of British Columbia cannot compete, when they get or ought to get a reasonable price.

Apples imported into Canada during last year cost, at the point of production, $2.41 a barrel. Added to that would be duty at the rate of 40 cents a barrel; and the cost of transportation from the orchards to the wholesale dealer would make the average price over $3 per barrel. In view of this fact, I do not see why these who have orchards in suitable districts in this country cannot engage in successful competition. I suppose that the effect of this measure will be that the producer in British Columbia will endeavour to raise his price to the producing centres near by. I suppose the hon. gentleman is right in saying that the measure is designed to save an industry; but is it good economics for one portion of the community to help another portion of the community to live? There is such a thing as carrying a national policy to extremes. There is at present a duty of 40 cents a barrel on apples.

Plus 7| per cent ad
valorem.

The total duty then would be 90 cents a barrel plus the 7| per cent special war duty, which is a very heavy rate on a commodity of this kind. It hardly seems businesslike to tax the consuming community to that extent. Why is it done? Simply to enable the producing sections of Canada to obtain a higher price for their apples than they would be able to secure if the consuming portions of the country were permitted to get them from an adjacent country at a lower cost. While we must have revenue, and it is not unreasonable to have incidental protection, it is very doubtful if we should impose a protective duty simply for the purpose of assisting any industry.

The hon. gentleman is
arguing against imposing a burden on one part of the community to help another. Would he favour the removal of the duty on coal, which would affect his own province?

Allow me to answer my
hon. friend in this way. The duty bn coal now is a very, very small percentage of the cost. When you impose a small duty, in view of the fact that we must have a revenue, it becomes a tariff for revenue purposes. But when you come down to the principle of protection,-and the hon. gentleman has admitted that this is a measure to save an industry and not a measure for revenue purposes-
The duty on coal is just about what we are asking on apples, ^between 25 per cent and 30 per cent.
Two blacks do not make a white.
Not at all.

I would be very glad to
see the duty on coal reduced to a reasonable rate. On such a commodity as apples, I certainly do not think that such a high rate of duty should be imposed as is now suggested. I believe that all commodities of this class, such as coal, in fact all natural products, ought to come into this country as far as possible free of duty. We might well say that coal is one of the products that should be brought into this country at the lowest possible rate of duty.

I wish to say a few words on the question of duty as it effects the Prairie Provinces. We in Alberta in particular, and it applies equally to the people of Saskatchewan, are forced to pay extremely high prices for our apples. Apples, it is generally recognized, are an essential article of food to-day, and anything that tends to increase the price naturally effects every one of the inhabitants of those provinces, because they all use apples. I have been dealing in apples for many years and know something about the prices. The statement made by hon. gentlemen opposite that the United States export their poor grades of apples-and that we in Alberta buy them is absolutely beside the truth, because in my experience' I never bought a box of apples that graded under No. 2 if I knew it; I have always bought No. 1 stock. We have to pay heavy transportation charges, and we cannot afford to pay freight on poor stuff, and that is the reason we cannot afford to buy apples from Ontario, although we have tried to do so year after year. I consider that we are an extremely patriotic people when in the face of the quality of fruit we have had to put up with from Ontario we still have faith to keep on trying year after year. We have been bitten so often that our patience is exhausted, and we are now forced to buy our fruit from the neighbouring states of Oregon and Washington.
You should try Quebec. That is where the best apples are grown; right in Rouville county.

We are not all millionaires, and to buy apples from Quebec would entail a cost of nearly $8 a barrel, which is

prohibitive. We have to pay, year in and year out, an average of $2.25 a box for apples.
Do you buy direct from the grower or from the jobber?
I have bought both ways. It is almost an impossibility to buy direct from the grower.
That is what I thought.

The growers in British Columbia and the American growers are all marketing now through exchanges, which is an especially good way of marketing fruit. But to my mind the real crux of the situation, so far as British Columbia is concerned, is their very poor marketing facilities. The statement of the hon. member for Lambton was rather grotesque, when he said that the growers of British Columbia and the growers of Ontario were uniting to have the products of British Columbia and the products of Ontario marketed by the grain growers of the three prairie provinces. The farmers might supply their own wants, I can quite conceive that, by buying direct from the exchanges in British Columbia, or in Ontario.

They are doing that
now.

But that does not affect the price of apples to any appreciable extent. We are still paying $6.75 to $7 a barrel in the prairie provinces. If, in the face of these exorbitant prices, this Government puts on an extra tariff of 50 cents a barrel to that extent it will add to our burdens, while, at the same time, the grower in British Columbia is not receiving a fair price for his apples. There is no question about that. He is getting, as hon. gentlemen opposite have stated, from 22 cents to 80 cents. According to the statement of the Minister of Finance, 80 cents is the average price paid for apples to the British Columbia grower, and that is a very high estimate, because the hon. member for Kootenay says that the price was 22 cents in 1914. I have a telegram from a prominent fruit grower in Salmon arm, who states that in 1914 the price to the grower
was 22 cents a box.
*
That refers to apples on ' the trees, before they are touched.

Yes; it may be the price before they are picked, but in 1915, his price was 80 cents a box picked. As a

matter of fact, I know that the farmer gets no more than 80 cents a box, and sometimes as low as 60 cents a box, when he takes his fruit, not from the tree, but into the exchange. The contention, therefore, that that price is for apples hanging on the tree is not very well founded. With a price of that kind, and a tariff of 30 cents, per box, the hon. member for Vancouver is not quite consistent when he says that they are quite willing to submit to a duty of 25 per cent, because, with apples costing around 60 cents a box, to produce or sell and1 with a tax of 30 cents, the grower would have more than 25 per cent protection. I have figured it out that the tariff at the present time, under the present growing conditions, represents very close to 40 per cent protection. If we could be certain that the producer in British Columbia would derive the benefit from this taxation, and that we, the consumers, would not have to pay any more, I am sure the people of the Prairie Provinces would be patriotic enough to purchase their fruit from British 'Columbia. But we have had experience in the past that does not hear out that contention. I claim that under the present proposed tariff we would not enjoy the benefit which has been suggested by the hon. gentlemen from British Columbia, and the consumers in the Prairie Provinces would be forced to pay, practically the whole of this enhanced duty. I want to warn the Minister of Finance of the effect it may have. To-day the farmers' organizations in the western provinces are looking so seriously on this question of increased taxation that they have passed a resolution pledging themselves to be patriotic to the Dominion of Canada by buying their-farm machinery in the United States, and paying the duty, so that the treasury of Canada will be enhanced, instead of paying the manufacturers of Eastern Canada an enhanced p'rice, which goes directly into then pockets, and not into the treasury of Canada. Be very careful lest the same condition arise in connection with the fruit industry.
M. J. G. TURRIFF (Assiniboia): After the discussion we have had this afternoon, the Ministpr of Finance would be well advised if he withdrew this resolution. I am very much of the opinion that if it was not the intention of the Minister of Finance to ufe this for the political advantage of the party in British Columbia, it certainly was the intention of some others. As I under-

stand the matter, the bulk of the apples grown and shipped from British Columbia are from the Kootenay country, the southern portion of British Columbia, and naturally it would be very much to the advantage of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell), who, we all regret, is not in his seat. I have no doubt that this duty was proposed largely in the interest, and at the request of, the Minister of Agriculture. We have heard a request from my hon. friend who represents Vancouver, for reciprocity between the Prairie Provinces and British Columbia. He pointed out, or some one else did, that large delegations came from British Columbia and asked that this duty be put on apples. The Minister of Finance lent a very ready ear to that demand for raising the duties, but when a much stronger delegation came from the Prairie Provinces, representing one hundred times the interest that exists in the applegrowing districts of British Columbia, and asked that duties be taken off, the Minister of Finance turned his deaf ear towards them.
Both ears were deaf.

Yes, both ears were deaf on that occasion. If my hon. friends from British Columbia want to develop the apple industry, why do they not follow the example of Alberta and Saskatchewan. When the farmers in these provinces wanted to develop the cheese-making and buttermaking industries, what did they do? They did not come to Ottawa and ask for extra duties to be put on. They appointed men, and paid them, to take charge of cheese factories and creameries on behalf of the farmers' organizations, and these establishments were run by the Government for two, or three, or four years. When they had been fairly well established, and were turning out good butter and good cheese, the Governments pulled out altogether; the farmers then ran the creameries and the butter factories themselves, and to-day they form a very important industry in those provinces. -	<
Is it not the fact that the butter makers in Alberta and Saskatchewan are protected by a tariff of 4 cents per pound?

My hon. friend is perfectly right, but will he point to a single instance where the farmers of these provinces asked for it? The farmers of the Western Prairie Provinces are not asking for higher duties; they are asking to have the duties taken off. They are prepared
to face any competition on the face of the earth in connection with the products they have to sell. If my hon. friends from British Columbia want to put the apple industry on a proper basis, let them go to their Provincial Government and ask them to take action along the lines of that taken by the Governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan in connection with butter and cheese. Do you think you are going to develop a national spirit in the Dominion of Canada when you set one province practically against another, or when you attempt to do so? My hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) tried to lead this House to believe that the farmers' organizations of the Prairie Provinces and the apple growers of British Columbia were getting together, and that the farmers' organizations of the prairies were going to distribute British Columbia apples. The Minister of Finance is treading on mighty dangerous ground when he keeps putting one burden after another on the prairie farmers. Let me read what has taken place within the last few days in this very connection. I read from the Manitoba Free Press of Wednesday, March 8:

Then it gives a list of those who were *present. I commend it to the Minister of Finance and my hon. friends who represents the apple growing districts in British Columbia. Just as sure as the sun will rise to-morrow, if this becomes law the British Columbia apple grower will sell fewer boxes of apples in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba than he is selling at the present time. enough? Yet, in face of that they come here and demand legislation that puts an added burden on the backs of the people of the prairie provinces. We know what has taken place in the last few days in British Columbia, and I am sure it was for the purpose of helping his friends there that the minister proposed this tariff to Parliament. The hon. member for Vancouver spoke about the small tax this would be and he said that the people he represents are in favour of developing the hinterland of British Columbia. A few years ago I was in Vancouver and I looked around the fruit stalls there to see what the British Columbia fruit was like. They said they could
bring in apples from the United States, pay the freight and duty and get them for less than the Okanagan Valley apples cost. My hon. friend also spoke about the quality of the apples. The Minister of Finance, in this matter, is undertaking to legislate especially for a very small number of people, because from a statement put before the House it appears that there were about 30,000 acres of land planted with apple trees and only a moderate number of these trees are bearing. The hon. member for South Oxford said that it was a shame to see so many American apples sold in Toronto, but no doubt these apples came in at a season when they were not getting Canadian apples. Why should millions of people in Canada, living in the cities and who do not grow apples, be forced to pay a higher price for apples in order to give a little more to land speculators or fruit growers in British Columbia? Is that fair, ip that reasonable, is that a national policy in any sense of the word, is it right to benefit a few, a very few, at the expense of the many? It seems to me that if that is the idea of this National Policy the time has about come when there should be a revision of ideas in connection with that policy. To my mind, the way to help the British Columbia apple grower is to make his conditions as nearly right as possible and leave the tariff out altogether.

It was a very favoured argument of hon. gentlemen on the Government side for many years prior to the reciprocity agreement, that we were ready to bring down our duties if the Americans would only do the same thing. Since then that duty has been materially reduced by the- American Government and to-day, if my information is correct, and if not I am sure my hon. friend's experts will, through the minister, set me right, the duty on apples going into the United States is 10 cents a barrel. The people of Canada were saying to the Government of the United States for many years :	If you will
reduce your duties we will reduce ours. The United States reduced their duty on apples to 10 cents a barrel three years ago, two years prior to the 6th of October last, and this Government now comes forward and says:	We are going to put the rate
on apples up to 90 cents a barrel. Ninety cents a barrel on apples is practically 100 per cent ad valorem. I venture to say that the farmers of Canada from the Atlantic to ' the Pacific do not get more than 90 cents a barrel for all the apples they sell at their farms. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance in order to benefit a small section of the country is forcing every man, woman, and child in the Dominion who eat apples to pay 100 per cent duty on the apples they consume. I leave it to you, Mr. Speaker,
I leave it to the members of the House to say whether that is a fair proposition, whether it is a reasonable proposition, whether it is a law that should be put on the statute-books. But apart altogether from the prairie consumers, why should dwellers in the large cities be compelled to pay a large increased price for apples? During many months of the year we import apples from the United States, and if this measure passes we shall have to pay the extra duty.
