I have a few words to say in the hope that the Minister of Finance will withdraw this particular clause. I do not say that my hope is very lively, but, knowing how fair-minded he is, I think that hope should be well grounded. It has been stated that it costs $1.08 a box to grow' apples in
British Columbia. That is at the rate of $3.24 a barrel. That is a very high price, and if it costs that much to grow apples in British Columbia, it would appear to me that they are not growing them as cheaply as they might; and if that is the case it is not fair that a few apple growers should be helped to maintain an over-expensive system of growing apples at the expense of the consumers generally, especially the consumers of the Prairie Provinces. There is no doubt that there has been improvement in Britisli Columbia apple culture, and in the handling of the crop. It strikes me that if our apple-growing friends in British Columbia would go on with this good work and arrange for the proper distribution of their crop, as well as the proper packing and shipping of it, instead of coming here and asking for more protection, it would be much better. If I believed that this extra duty would really benefit the apple growers of British Columbia, or even that they would get a reasonable, share of it, I would not be so strongly opposed to it. But I do not believe that the actual grower is going to get very much benefit out of this duty.
There is another ground on which we of the Prairie Provinces have reason to complain. Some hon. members, including, I think, the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), pointed out that the apple growers of the states adjoining British Columbia ship their poor quality apples into the Prairie Provinces-that 85 percent of the	apples shipped into
western Canada were of No. 3 grade. If we in the West have to eat the poor grades of apples from Oregon, what is to be our position under this duty? This will enable the British Columbia, Ontario, and Nova Scotia apple growers to ship their good qualities of apples to foreign markets, and then, behind this prohibitive duty of 100 per cent, compel us to buy the poor grades.

Will the hon. gentleman permit me to correct him? What I said was that 85 per cent of the apples imported into the Northwest were of C grade, which is equal to our No. 2. I did not say they were a poor grade. On the contrary, they are a very good grade of apples.

I accept the correction; but the argument remains the same. If a duty of practically 100 per cent is put upon apples, the growers vrill be able to ship those of good quality to outside markets and force the poor qualities on the people of the West who are compelled to import apples either from British Columbia, On-

tario, or the United' States. We in that country are willing to pay and we do pay, a good price for apples, but we want to be in a position to command apples of good quality; we do not want the ' Government practically to take us by the throat and tel] us that we must use the' refuse apples while the good ones are shipped elsewhere.
As I have stated before, for many of the people in my own constituency this will represent a duty of almost 300 per cent. Carloads and carloads of apples come into the stations south of the boundary line, in art ordinary year when there is a good crop, and my constituents can go and buy apples at 25 cents a bushel shovelled in bulk out of the car. A man will buy 30 bushels at 25 cents, or 75 cents a barrel. Under this clause, he will be called upon for a duty of 90 cents on these apples which cost 75 cents. This is an inducement to the people of that country to smuggle. Why should the Government go out of their way to make it almost imperative for my constituents to do smuggling?
In view of the facts that we have been brought out in this discussion, I would ask the Minister of Finance to withdraw this proposal. If he will noit withdraw it on economic grounds, will he not withdraw it on national grounds? It was pointed out by my hon. friend from Strathcona (Mr. Douglas) that the farmers' organizations of the prairies, at their annual meetings or at meetings specially called, had passed a resolution calling on their members not to buy Canadian farm implements, but to buy American farm implements and let the money go into the treasury for the purposes of the war instead of going into the pockets of the manufacturers. We have the same farmers' organizations this week protesting against this duty on apples and calling on their members to buy American apples and pay the money into the treasury. I want to tell the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance that they are bringing on a most unsatisfactory state of feeling in Canada between the East and the West, and are deliberately driving the wedge horrie. The action of the Government in this pin-pricking policy-because it does not amount to anything in dollars-i? calculated to have far-reaching effects. On these grounds I hold that the Minister of Finance should leave this apple business alone. The duty is high enough, surely. It was stated here this afternoon that in British Columbia a few years ago the farmers got 22 cents a box for their apples. As the duty was 39

cents a barrel, this meant a duty of 13 *cents a box. Was not that duty high enough? And even when apples are worth 50 or 60 cents a box, is not a duty of 13 cents a box-with the additional duty of 7J per cent ad valorem that was added last year-quite enough?
I do not know what the apple growers of British Columbia can be thinking about when they want to have a duty of 100 per cent. It is all right for them, perhaps, but what about the people who have to pay it- not only the people of the Prairie Provinces, but the consumers and workers in every village, town and city in this broad Dominion? Again I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, in the interest of this country and in the interest of the national policy which he is so fond of advocating, to withdraw this item. I am sure that if he does that he will be doing something good for Canada. Throughout the West a feeling of dissatisfaction is growing strongly and rapidly with regard to the efforts that are being made to tax unfairly the people of that country.	*

The statement has been made to-day that the apples which are brought in from the United States are second and third grades. If that is so then we in the West who eat them can say that they compare very favourably with the first grades from British Columbia. I am not going to reflect upon British Columbia apples, but I do say that the men who reflect on the British Columbia apples are those who assert that the apples we get from the United States are of poor grade, because if they are then the first grade apples in the United States must be dandies. The British Columbia and the Western States apples are well packed and, even in quality as we get them in the boxes, and that is'why British Columbia and United States fruit has a preference over Ontario fruit in *the western provinces. I say it with regret, because I come from an apple growing district in Ontario, that Ontario apples are not even, that the best apples are at the top, and that sometimes there are some pretty mean apples in the middle. Perhaps, if we have a few more elections like that which took place in Peel we will in future get better apples from Ontario. In my hotel here in Ottawa the other day I was eating an apple and I asked the waiter if he could find out where it came from, because it was such a good one, and he told me it was a British Columbia apple. Why is it that in this very province British Columbia is supplying the hotels with apples?
Because the apples are better.
Of course they are; that is right.

I want to say in answer to the hon. gentleman that the most careful inspection of Ontario apples is going on every year during the packing season, and the man in charge of the fruit association is giving his very best attention to that work. I am, therefore, sure that it would not be possible for inferior fruit to be shipped to the Northwest. At any rate, I would hope not.

I wish to correct the
statement of the hon. member [DOT].Mr. Ar.n-strong) that the apple trade of the Prairie Provinces is in the hands of the United
States fruit trust. I say that is absolutely not the fact. In my own constituency there are merchants in the different towns who bring in fruit by the carload, who send to Ontario, British Columbia, and the United States and get prices, and they buy whenever they can get the right quality of fruit to the best advantage, and they sell it where they like, and they have no connection with, and are under no control of any United States fruit trust.
Mr. J. E.ARMSTRONG: The hon. gentleman has made the statement that they have not brought in apples from the United States, but merely from Ontario and British Columbia; that is a very different question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Listening to the observations of hon. gentlemen opposite, 1 have been thinking that there has been much cry and little wool. It seems to me we have had a good deal of talk about a very small matter. In order that hon. gentlemen opposite, who have taken part in the debate, and who appear to be really concerned about the imposition of this tax, may sleep to-night, I would like to assure them that even on the basis of the present importation, assuming that the extra duty will have to be paid, which will not be the case, in the very next item which we shall consider, namely, the item in reference to crude petroleum in which the duty on heavy distillates used largely by the farmers in the West is reduced from two and a half to one-half of a cent per gallon, the reduction more than equals, as far as the farmers of the West are concerned, the extra duty upon apples.

You had better not
mix crude oil and apples.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You cannot mix them, but I mention that in order to relieve the consciences of hon. gentlemen opposite. While there is a small increase on apples, really inconsequential as far as money payment is concerned, there is a reduction in the next item that will more than equalize it.

I would like to ask the minister if there is not also an increase in one of the oil items. While it may not apply so much to the farmers, and while it applies particularly to the railways, if you increase the cost of fuel oil to the railways, you increase the cost tcv the farmer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend would raise that point on the next

item. I do not believe myself that the Railway Commission would,, on that argument, order an increase in freight rates.
Perhaps the minister would tell us to what extent crude oil is used in agriculture and in other industries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When we reach the next item.

When the minister was discussing this increase in the duty on apples in his Budget speech he gave the impression that it was a provision especially for the apple-growing industry of British Columbia, but from the course of the discussion to-day I should incline to the view' that instead of this item being specially intended to improve the position of the apple grower in British Columbia, it was simply following out the general line of policy which has been pursued by this Government since it took office, in the way of placing more completely in the 9 p.m. hands of their friends the middlemen, an important article of the food of the people. As has been Observed by speakers to-d,ay, especially on the other side of the House, this duty applies to the whole of Canada. It affects not only the people of the Prairie Provinces as consumers, but the people of all Canada as consumers, and, according to our friends who come .from apple-growing districts in . other provinces, it affects not only the apple growers of British Columbia, but the apple growers of the whole Dominion. Therefore we are bound to consider this legislation not as a local, but as a national question. Speaking of this increased duty in his Budget speech, the minister said:
We regard this duty as indispensably necessary for the preservation of the apple-growing industry of Canada, and particularly that of British Columbia.
So far as British Columbia is concerned, the apple-growing industry has grown from
200.000	_ barrels four years ago to nearly
500.000	barrels last year.
What w'as the cause of that increase?

It does not concern me what the cause was: the fact is what I am concerned with. And the fact is that the apple-growing industry grew' from 200,000 barrels four years ago to nearly 800,000 barrels last year. That is not disputed. We also find 'that the country at large ex-

ported over 1,000,000 barrels of apples, and imported only a little over a quarter of a million. Therefore, whether we take it in regard to the industry throughout Canada as a whole, or in regard to the industry as respects British Columbia alone, of all industries in Canada the apple industry seems to stand* least in need of special tariff legislation or special tariff consideration. Canada is an apple exporter, and if the course of trade were permitted to go in the natural channels and in the natural way, the price to the producer would be ruled by the export price; and, that being the case, the producer would not expect to benefit, and would not benefit by the imposition of an extra duty. The only purpO'Se of an increase in duty where the article which it is proposed to protect is an article of export rather than of import is for the purpose of enabling those who are in control of the trade to take advantage of fictitious or artificial prices at the expense of both the producer and the consumer. Just as in the Canadian milling industry the miller buys his wheat from the Canadian producer at a less price than his competitor in the United States, and sells his finished product to the Canadian consumer at a higher price, so, by this legislation it is proposed to put those who are in control of the apple trade in. Canada in the position of paying what they please to the producer, and charging what they please to the consumer.
This has been spoken of as a trifling matter. -But at this time, when the country is compelled to assume ever-increasing and already enormous financial obligations, when the necessity of increasing the efficient production of the people by lightening their burdens is the first duty of the Government of this country, it is no trifling matter to bring forward legislation for which there is no reason or excuse except that it is for the purpose of enabling those engaged in the apple trade still more thoroughly to control both the buying and the selling markets of this country. This is a matter affecting not only the prairies of the West, but every citizen of this Dominion. This legislation affects the citizens of Toronto, and Ottawa, and Montreal, surrounded as they are by apple orchards, just as much as it affects the citizens of the prairies of the West, because its purpose is to put the supply of his requirements under the control of an organization that .will take more out of him than it can take to-day.

It is said the consumer will not have to ipay more. But it is also said, on this side of itlhe House, .and it cannot be denied, that if the consumer does not have to pay more there is no possible purpose in the legislation. Fo,r the producer certainly is not going to get more unless either the consumer pays more or there is some readjustment of the conditions intervening between the producer and the consumer, and this latter is neither contemplated nor suggested by this legislation. At the present time, in the province of Alberta, the retail price of apples is approximately $2.25 for a box containing 40 pounds of apples. That is equal to $6.75 a barrel. Anybody must admit that that is a good stiff price for apples, and everybody will say that if the producer got his fair share out of that price he would be doing very well and would not need to ask for beneficial legislation.	The apple orchards of British
Columbia are situated within between four hundred and five hundred miles of the city of Edmonton. At Salmon Arm, on the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway, during the past season, the apple growers received 80 cents a, box for their apples-for which apples we in Edmonton paid $2.25 a box. The year before, these growers received 22 cents a box-and we in Edmonton paid the same, $2.25. At Penticton, last year, the growers of apples got an average of 85 cents a box, ajxd the year before the average was 40 cents a box. Now, Penticton is a hundred miles further from Edmonton than Salmon Arm, and it is not on the main line, and yet the grower at Penticton received a better price than the grower at Salmon Arm.
I think there is a misunderstanding there. The price in one case is for the apples on the tree, and in the other case for the apples boxed and ready for shipment.
Did the price of 22 cents a box include the box?
No.
Did the price of 80 cents a box include the box?
Yes.

Then, we will have to take the opinion of the man in the business, which information came by wire yesterday in reply to an inquiry. His telegram reads : 11-3
Salmon Arm fruit ranchers selling through Okanagan United growers, received for No. 1 apples, 1915, 80 cents per box net. In 1914, 22 cents per box, net.
If the box is included in one case it is included in the other, and if it is excluded in one it is excluded in both. The hon. gentleman can have it either way he likes, but he cannot have it one way in the one case and the other way in the other case. I have a telegram from Penticton, dated yesterday, which says:
Apples per box, No. 1, 85 cents last season ; year before, 40 cents.
The point I make is that the price we pay at Edmonton, the consumer's price does not govern the price received by the producer, as matters stand to-day. And how it is expected that the addition of 30 cents a barrel to the protective duty is going to better that condition, I cannot undei-stand, when no provision is made for securing any change. If to-day the transportation companies and distributing agencies take the difference between 80 cents and $2.25, are they not going to take the difference if the duty is increased by 30 cents a barrel? There is no manner of doubt that the transportation companies and distributing agencies to-day take an undue toll from the producer and from the consumer. They do that under a protective advantage of approximately 60 cents a barrel. Will the Minister of Finance or the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Green) tell us that they are not going to pursue 'the same course if their advantage is increased by 30 cents a barrel? Will the hon. member for Kootenay or anybody else tell us how the addition to the duty of 30 cents a barrel will make them less likely to take advantage of the producer at one end and of the consumer at the other?

It is going to make this difference, that the producer will have the market to himself, and will be able to make better market arrangements. He will get into direct communication, and will deal direct with the consumer.
If he can do that with an additional duty of 10 cents a box-for that is what this additional duty will amount to -why cannot he do it without that addition?

For the simple reason that at any time the growers in the Northwestern States may flood the market with consignment cars at prices as low as 30 cents a box. Hundreds of carloads are



shipped in in that way. So that the grower in the Okanagan valley has no.t got and cannot establish a market to which he oan regularly ship his fruit, because he does not know what, moment he will get a wire shutting off his shipments. Nobody can do business under those conditions.

I can assure my hon. friend that if these remarkably cheap apples came to Edmonton, no Edmonton citizen ever got the benefit of them. We were paying the standard prices for apples, wherever they came from.
Perhaps they came from the American fruit trust.

The American fruit trust is the Canadian fruit trust, as far as we are concerned; it is absolutely one and the same thing. The fruit trust that is .squeezing the Okanagan grower and the Edmonton buyer at 60 cents a barrel protection can squeeze them just as much at 90 cents a barrel protection, and certainly it will do so. Is it not a fact that the year before last fruit was rotting on the ground in the Okanagan?
It is.

Is it not a fact that we were paying $2.25 for apples at that very time? Yet the Minister of Finance proposes to put 30 cents a barrel additional advantage in the hands of the American fruit trust. They cannot do worse to the grower in the Okanagan than let his fruit rot on the ground, but they can take 30 cents a barrel more out of us; that is the only purpose that will be served.

If the producers in British Columbia and Ontario, through their Fruit Growers Associations, make definite arrangements with the farmers' distributing agencies in- the western provinces, is there any possibility of any such condition arising in the western provinces as that to which my horn, friend has referred?

I do not know what may occur as between the apple growers and the farmers' associations. I only know what is occurring now, and what has occurred in the past. The increase of the duty by 30 cents a barrel is not going substantially to change the conditions except to the advantage of the trust. My hon. friend says that if this duty is increased the apple grower of British Columbia will be able to market his own fruit in the West. I do not know whether he will or not, but, accord-

ing to the figures, it seems to me that he is perfectly able to do that now. We will allow him 80 cents a box for his apples; it is not claimed that he gets any more.
It costs $1.08 a box to produce them.

That is not our fault. If it costs him so much to produce them, the only answer is that he is not growing apples in the right place. The apples exported from Canada, over a million barrels, are valued at $2.40 a barrel, or 80 cents a box. If the British Columbia apple grower cannot produce apples at the price at which the Nova Scotia apple growers produce for export, then he is working under wrong conditions and has no right to expect the people of the rest of Canada to maintain him in an industry the location of which he has not chosen wisely. As to my hon. friend's suggestion that apples cannot be produced in British Columbia at less than $1.08 a box, I should be out of order if I characterized it as absurd; certainly it is not such as coincides with my view. If there is any place on the North American continent where apples can be grown more cheaply than in the district of Salmon Arm, I have never seen it. There is no reason why the British Columbia apple grower cannot compete on equal terms with the grower of apples in Washington and Oregon.
They are all going broke in Washington and Oregon.
My hon. friend says they are all going broke. Well, they are selling apples, and that is what the consumer of Canada wants.
It is the receivers who are selling the apples.
The cost of package and packing is 48 cents a box.
My hon. friend will have to accept my protest against his figures. They are just as far out of the way as his assertion in regard to the cost of growth.
My figures are those of the Fruit Growers' Association of British Columbia, and of Prof. Lewis, an expert of the United States Government.

If it costs the British Columbia grower so much to grow his apples and so much to pack them, he ought to be in some other business; he has no right to ask the people of Canada to maintain him in a losing industry. As a matter of fact, we are to-day paying 65 cents a box for apples in excess of a fair price, allowing everybody everything to which he is entitled. If that is not a sufficient margin to enable the Fruit Growers' Association of British Columbia to find their own markets on the prairies, it simply argues that they have not enterprise, or that they are under control and management that dpes them absolutely no credit. They have no right to ask this Parliament to tax the whole population of Canada in order that the fruit combine and the transportation interests, not the fruit grower, shall get more money.
I have given the transportation rate at 38 cents a box. That is 38 cents for carrying 50 pounds of freight for 400 miles. Wheat is carried from Winnipeg to Port Arthur over 400 miles, at 6 cents a bushel: that is, 10 cents per cwt. It costs 7i times as much to bring the same weight of apples from Salmon Arm to Edmonton as it costs to take a bushel of wheat from Winnipeg to Port Arthur, the same distance. Now, admitting that apples should pay a higher rate than wheat, we do not admit that 74 times as much is a reasonable rate. The fact is that the apple industry has been exploited from start to finish, just as the mining industry and many others have been. The land speculator has expected to make a fortune out of the price of land, the transportation companies have expected to make huge profits out of the transport of freight, and then the fruit dealer comes in and expects, and realizes his expectation, to make more than the transportation company or the U3J
fruit grower out of the unfortunate consumer. My friend the Minister of Finance proposes to legislate to add 30 cents a barrel to that tariff condition which enables this robbery to be perpetrated, not by the unfortunate man who is growing fruit in British Columbia, but by the fruit dealer and the transportation companies who handle the transportation and distribution of the fruit.
When the Minister of Finance mentioned this proposed fruit duty in his Budget speech, he spoke of the fruit industry of British Columbia. It is true that there is a fruit industry of British Columbia, but it is in a very small part of British Columbia; and the greater part of that province is in exactly the same condition as the Prairie West in regard to the production of fruit. The miners of Fernie in the constituency of my hon. friend (Mr. Green) the constituents of my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), the constituents of my hon. friend for Victoria (Mr. Barnard), and those of my hon. friend from Comox-Atlin (Mr. Clements) will all pay this extra price. My hon. friend who represents the miners of Nanaimo (Mr. Shepherd) will have to explain to those miners why he has been instrumental in adding to their cost of living, which already has climbed so high, in the name of the fruit growers of British Columbia-who will not receive the benefit of the duty that is being imposed. This duty is just as much for the benefit of the railway companies and the fruit combine as the duty on flour is a duty on behalf of the railway companies and the milling industry and no't on behalf of the farmer who produces the wheat. It is in the last degree objectionable that the attempt should be made to show that one section of the country must live at the cost of all the rest. If that is a fact, it is an unfortunate condition. But it is not a fact and never was a fact. The fruit-growing area of British Columbia is well adapted to the production of fruit. It is well situated in relation to markets, and if it is not to-day prosperous it is not because of a lack of natural conditions for production, or location in relation to advantageous markets, but it is because it is in the same position as the grain-growing industry of the West in relation to the milling industry. It is in the hands of a combine which exercises the advantage that the tariff gives it to levy an unjust toll upon the consumer on the one hand and upon the producer on the other, and every addition that is made.

to the tariff increases the power of the combine and its ability to increase its unjust toll.
267a. Crude petroleum in Its natural state, *7900 specific gravity or heavier at 60 degrees temperature, when imported by oil refiners to be refined in their own factories-British preferential tariff, 5 per cent; intermediate tariff, 7J per cent; general tariff, 7J per cent.

Would the minister give rather a comprehensive explanation of the effect of this change in the tariff, perhaps discussing both items at the same time. There is a reduction in the tariff, which some hon. gentlemen are at a loss to understand as expressed in the amendment.

Does the item include
gasolene?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I will tell my hon. friend later what it does not include. The best way to describe the article we are dealing with now, because this oil schedule is quite technical and complicated, is to describe it as fuel oil.

There are certain traction engines which are advertised through-

out the West as being oil fuel engines; is it the oil for these engines to which the minister refers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is an increase from about one-third of a cent to one-half cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

It is difficult to separate the items, to which we have been referring, from other items that are included in the trade and commerce returns.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Fuel oil for locomotives and steamships, and for heating purposes; in fact, it is fuel just as coal is.
I understand it is also used in the manufacture of munitions.
What is the cost of that oil to railway and steamship companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From 2 to 4 cents a gallon.
Do I understand that the duty on gasolene is not changed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no change as regards gasolene.

I understand from what the Solicitor General said that there was a change.
Sir' THOMAS WHITE: There have been several mis-statements in the course of the debate. I did not hear what the Solicitor General said, but, for example an hon. gentleman on the other side thought the change referred to illuminating oil, and! he made a rather touching domestic reference to the child being deprived of light when going to bed. The child will be able to go to bed as usual, because there is no increase in regard to illuminating oil. Not only will there be additional revenue, but I believe the change will be of some material advantage to the great coal industry in British Columbia.
In what way?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from Halifax knows how Nova Scotia treasures the duty upon coal, and how important that is regarded by all good Nova Scotians. So this duty will, I think, have an important effect upon the coal mining industry of British Columbia.

Those who have hitherto consumed oil, must cease using as much in the future, if any benefit is to accrue to the coal industry. The minister informed us that this particular oil fuel
was consumed by the railways and steamships on the Pacific coast. Which of these two will be consumers of coal hereafter- the railways, or the steamships, or both?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that it is not probable that the steamship companies will discontinue the use of fuel oil; nor do I think that the railways are likely to discontinue its use. But for the future, I think the tendency will be to use coal more than fuel oil; that is to say, there will be more of an equality, so to speak, in the use of coal and fuel oil. I may say that, of late years, the use of coal in the province of British Columbia, to take that province as an example, has steadily declined, while the certificates show, on the other hand, that the use of fuel oil has been on the increase. The figures are rather startling.

Some people say that the coal of British Columbia is not satisfactory for steamship purposes. Does the minister know whether that is so or not? Why has there been a general increase in the use of fuel oil?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the reason is that they have been able to get the fuel oil so cheaply. It has come in free of duty. My hon. friend knows that in the province of Ontario there has frequently been an agitation by the manufacturers for free coal, but, as I said to my hon. 'friend from Halifax, Nova Scotia is very much interested in the duty on coal. Fuel oil has been on the free list, and the use of it has greatly increased in British Columbia. On the other hand, as I have stated, the amount of coal used has steadily declined, and coal mining is one of the most important industries of British Columbia. The production of coal on Vancouver Island since 1911 has been:
Gross tons.
1911		 1,443,000
1912		 1,250,000
1913		 730,000
1914		 814,000
1915		 786,000
So that in 1915 the production of coal on Vancouver Island was about half that of 1911.
Would the minister give the statistics as to the importation of fuel oil during these years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The difficulty is in separating them, but I will give some figures which will throw light upon it.

While the deputy is finding those figures, I might just say that the duty will be quite a heavy tax on the Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian Pacific, while it will add revenue to the Canadian Northern men who own the coal mines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am told,
although I do not know, that the Canadian Northern men do not own the coal mines.
I am afraid you were told wrongly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: However, I may say to my hon. friend that in the last few years we have received a great many memorials from the coal mining districts of British Columbia, boards of trade, and others who are very much interested in this subject. The amount which will be paid by the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk Pacific with respect to this duty will not be large for such corporations. There is another consideration I mentioned at the outset that weighed in a very considerable measure with me, and that is that we shall derive a revenue of $500,000 from this tax.
From what particular source?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That raises a very fine economic question as to who pays the duty. Some would argue that the oil producers in the United States would pay the duty, and others would argue that the railway and steamships companies, and some other interests in British Columbia, would pay it.
What do you think about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would raise another question, such as the question as to who pays for the German navy. But we would get very far afield if we took up that question.

Through what medium
does the minister expect to get it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The customs
office.

From whom does the
customs office expect to get it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the same question again.

It is interesting to consider the effect it will have on different interests. I do not imagine the Grand Trunk Pacific wrill be specially hit by the new war

tax, but the Canadian Pacific will be. I do not imagine the Canadian Northern will be struck very, hard by it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do you not think they will have 7 per cent on capital?

I am inclined to think
not at the present time. But the two other companies that are using oil for fuel in the mountains, for the protection of the forests and possibly for their own benefit, will have to pay an extra price for their oil, or else they will have to buy coal from the Canadian Northern or the interests that own the Canadian Northern. I am not sure it will work out just as the minister expects. If the revenue is to be derived it will be derived from one interest, the Canadian Pacific, which is being pretty heavily taxed for war purposes anyway on account of its position financially. If a revenue is not to be derived from this company it may be because they do not use oil, that they will do away with their oil consumers and use the coal that their competitors have to sell. I am not sure that my hon. friend is not working out a plant for one interest as against another.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am quite sure I am not working a plant and that I expect to get $500,000 of revenue.
Mr. GRAHAM Then they will not be burning coal; they will stick to oil.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian Northern, if they use oil, can well afford to pay this tax. At all events, I shall not lose any sleep about their ability to pay this or any other tax.

speechtext:

196,000,000 gallons of petroleum, crude fuel and gas oils were imported last year and about one-half of that would be fuel oil. In round numbers that would be 100,000,000 gallons as I stated.

speechtext: The duty collected on this importation amounted to $960. If that is. correct my hon. friend is not going to get very much money out of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken. The articles to which hp refers are not embraced in this item. It is item 267 that we are dealing with. There is a large consumption of fuel oil in Ontario in connection with the manufacture, among other things, of munitions.

If the purpose oi this tariff change is to secure revenue, it, would be more favourably considered by the House than if it had another object. I think the minister should instruct the House as to whether this change is to he permanent or whether it is his intention to remit the taxation, and revert to the statu quo after the war, or the necessities as to increased revenue have passed. There are many disadvantages, from the standpoint of British Columbia even, in changing the tariff upon oil. The figures which the minister submitted to us about the coal industry would indicate a gradual falling off in coal production, but I assume that that corresponds to the general decline in business in British Columbia during the past few years. I would expect, although I cannot establish the statement by any authority, that all lines of industry had declined in that province during the past few years and accordingly coal production has fallen off. With the resumption of British Columbia's former prosperity, which I hope will come some time in the near future, we probably will see the coal production back to the old figures. But this particular product, fuel oil, we are informed, is used by steamships and railways and it will be interesting to inquire why they adopt that method of power in preference to coal.
As regards the Pacific coast, I understand that most of the tonnage entering Victoria and Vancouver use fuel oil; at least, a great many of the steamers do, which is not true of'shipping on the Atlantic coast. Fuel oil is a more efficient and cheaper power producer than coal. Most of the freighters built in Great Britain during the last few years have been equipped for fuel oil in preference to coal, and we shall see more of that in the future than in the past. Now, if shipping on the Pacific coast uses oil as power because of its greater efficiency and lesser cost, it is not desirable from the standpoint of the ports of British
Columbia to compel shipping to use the more expensive power. I understand that a delegation from British Columbia has been, or is coming, to Ottawa to urge the Government to assist in providing tonnage for the Pacific coast, which they are sorely in need of at the present time. If that is true, it is not sound business to increase the operating costs of ships by competing them to use a power which is more costly than fuel oil, and also less desirable from many other standpoints. I do not think it will be conferring any advantage upon British Columbia to compel them to use coal instead of fuel oil on their ships and railways. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has stated, and it has been stated on a great many occasions in the past, that at . least the Canadian Pacific railway have been using fuel oil in the mountain region for some years, mainly to prevent fires, which of course
10 p.m. are more likely to occur when coal is used. I understand that they made this change largely at the suggestion of the governmental authorities oi British Columbia, owing to the frequent fires caused by locomotives, and which resulted in great losses to the lumbering industry in that province. If, a few years ago, public opinion in British Columbia compelled the Canadian Pacific railway to adopt fuel oil as its power, I do not think it is fair to do anything which might compel the road to revert to coal, as that would increase its operating costs.
We have had a lengthy discussion this afternoon and evening about apples, and the representatives of British Columbia have claimed the Prairie Provinces as their natural market. They startled the House, and the country I imagine, with the figures they gave off the cost _pf production of apples. To those figures there is to be added the cost of freight. Now, if this change in the tariff means an addition to the power cost of railways, I suppose that in some way or other this extra cost will be charged against the traffic, and just as likely as not apples will have to bear its share along with the other commodities carried by the railway. So in that respect you would be conferring no advantage on British Columbia, even if this change in the tariff indirfectly caused a little increase in the consumption of British Columbia coal. If the minister is proposing this change in the tariff for the purpose of revenue only, I can see that he has established a case, although I do not say that it
.1800

cannot be well answered. But if he proposes this change upon other grounds I think it is not reasonably supported, by all the facts and circumstances, and I do not think the change he proposes is justified or justifiable. I think we should have a declaration from the minister now, whether or not he proposes this as a revenue measure. It does look as if it were intended as a permanent measure. If so, we on this side of the House should he inclined to look at it from an altogether different angle from what we should if it were just a temporary measure, and for revenue purposes only.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I have already stated we should derive a revenue of about $500,000 from this change. That is a substantial amount and it' is very desirable that we should obtain it at this time. T also stated that the change would confer an incidental protection which I think is much needed by the coal mining industry of British Columbia. As to making statements whether a tariff change is permanent or otherwise, I think it exceedingly inexpedient for a Finance Minister to make any such statement, and I believe it has never been done. The tariff of this country is revised and changed from time to time, and when changes are made they are announced in the Budget in the usual way. This 1 suggested change will give revenue and will, I believe, be of benefit to the coal mining industry of British Columbia. It seems to me that the two reasons I have given are pretty good grounds for this change and I believe it will meet with public approval.
Mr F. H. SHEPHERD (Nanaimo). T'.r hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) evidently fears that the proposed tax of half a cent a gallon on fuel oil will be a hardship and have disastrous results. I may tell my hon. friend from Halifax that the imposition of the half-a-eent duty does pot bring coal on a parity with fuel oil as it existed previous to the invasion of fuel oil in the province in the year 1910. I will endeavour to treat this-matter as impartially as I can. Naturally I represent the industry of my constituency, namely, the coal mining industry of Vancouver Island. The invasion of fuel oil has very seriously affected the industry of Western British Columbia and incidentally of Eastern British Columbia; so much so that if the importation of fuel oil continues on the same scale as for the last five years, the very

extensive coal mining industry of Vancouver Island will be seriously threatened. If the committee will bear with me I will give some figures which will throw considerable light on the matter and supply information which from the questions that have been asked I presume hon. gentle-paen have not at hand. Now, various theories have been put forth as to why the invasion of fuel oil occurred. One of the favorite reasons is that it was largely due to the labour troubles .on Vancouver Island. But that is not the case. It is true that the labour troubles in Vancouver Island may have accelerated the use of fuel oil, but by no means is it responsible for the enormous invasion that has occurred. The labour troubles commenced in September, 1912, but one company only was affected until May, 1913,
when the strike spread to the other mines. But shortly afterwards the mines where the strike started were working to almost their full capacity, and at no time was the whole of the output cut off. The importation of fuel oil rose from over
7,000,000 gallons in 1911 to 20,000,000 gallons in 1912. The labour troubles did not commence until the year was well advanced.; therefore, the output of coal was not seriously curtailed. The true reason for the increased importation was the rapid extension of oil-burning installations, which was in keeping with plans, conceived and determined upon long before the labour troubles of Vancouver island commenced. This is especially true of railway and transportation companies. The operators asked not that the proposed duty should be prohibitive, but that it should be sufficient to place the coal mining industry upon something like a parity with its competitors. It is not intended or supposed that the large consumers, or, for that matter, any of the consumers who have gone to the expense of making oil-burning installations, will return to the use of coal. But we do believe that the imposition of the half cent per gallon duty on fuel oil will act as a deterrent upon those who otherwise would have entered upon the use of fuel oil.
What is the cost of the imported fuel oil?

The cost of imported fuel oil delivered at the wharf in Vancouver is about two cents per gallon. It requires about three and a half barrels of oil to equal one ton of Vancouver island coal. The cost, therefore, of the oil equivalent to one ton of Vancouver island coal would be approximately $2.80. The cost of the two fuels, one on the wharf at Vancouver, and the other at the pit mouth in Nanaimo, would be $2.80 for the oil and approximately $4 for the coal. Of course, there is the gulf to cross, and that would add a little to the cost of the coal. The committee can readily see, therefore, the enormous advantage that accrues to the railway companies and other users of oil by reason of the cheaper cost. It is no severe impost upon the users of fuel oil to pay one-half cent per gallon, as they were deriving an enormous advantage by the use of fuel oil which they did not enjoy previous to its importation. Had the duty imposed been such as to place the cost of fuel to these users above the original cost of coal, there might, as has been suggested by the hon. member for

Halifax, have been some injustice; but such is not the case. I have reason to believe, of course, that the large users would naturally object even to the imposition of this one-half cent a gallon. When you come to consider that the duty not only is a source of revenue at a time when it is much needed, but also will tend to preserve one of the most important industries in British Columbia; and when you consider how generously these transportation companies have been treated by the Government, you would naturally think that they would accept graciously this increase of duty, especially as it means the preservation of an industry of which they themselves are beneficiaries. Large coal mining centres must contribute to the railway companies by freight, transportation of passengers and otherwise, and it would seem not to he business policy to endeavour by selfish sentiment, if I may use the expression, to prevent an industry like the coal mining industry in British Columbia from enjoying full prosperity. Speaking of the generous manner in which the railway companies have been treated, I believe it is a fact that in British Columbia double freight and passenger rates are charged. There is reason for this. British Columbia is a country of physical and geographical difficulties. The cost of the railway in the first instance was great; the cost of operating is great. In this connection I may say that the railway companies operating from the state of Washington, south of the boundary line, who have railways built across the alluvia] flats of the Fraser river, do the very same thing. The moment they cross the international boundary they charge double rates. Their engines are fired with fuel oil, which is probably put on in the state of Washington; these engines come into the province and return to the United States in due course. They will not pay this half-cent duty, although the double charges are imposed. I commend this to the consideration of the minister, because this may be a matter which he has not covered in his proposal to collect a half-cent duty on all imported fuel oil. Of course, you could not collect a tax upon fuel for motive power on board a steamer making a trip into a port and going out again. Still, the fact remains that these engines run into British Columbia with fuel oil and will continue to do so.

Supposing a tariff is imposed against oil used in the locomotive, as the hon. member suggests should be 
done. Would the railway company continue to use oil and pay the duty, or would they change engines at a divisional point near the international boundary line?
I am not pressing the matter; the revenue would be so small that it need not be considered.

But it would not serve the interests of my hon. friend's constituents at all if they continued to pay the duty. It would do the coal mines of British Columbia no good unless the people of the province ceased using oil for power. To accomplish the purpose suggested by my hon. friend, the railways will have to change engines at the divisional point nearest the international boundary line, and consume coal from that point on to Vancouver.

They might change
engines. My object in giving that little illustration is that these railway companies are enjoying the enormous advantages granted to the Canadian Pacific railway for building through rugged countries, while they have built their railroads through comparatively easy country.

I understand all that. But my hon. friend evidently desires the imposition of this duty for a specific purpose, and he is quite frank about it. That purpose is to lessen the importation of fuel oil and to increase the (production of provincially produced coal. At the same time he reminds the committee that this duty is not prohibitive. If it is not at all prohibitive, the result will be that we may get a revenue, but oil will be consumed just as usual and there will be no increase in the consumption of coal, and no one will benefit unless it be the Minister of Finance.

I am afraid my hon. friend has a short memory. I shall read again:
The operators do not ask that the proposed duty should be prohibitive, blit the duty should be sufficient to place the coal mining Industry upon something like a parity with its competitors.
And I followed those remarks by stating that it would not be a prohibitive duty but would be a deterrent duty that would deter those who had otherwise contemplated going into the use of fuel oil, and would therefore -arrest the enormous invasion at this point, and therein the coal miners would be benefited.
All who are now in will stay in, and no more will come in.

Precisely. And the invasion will be arrested at this point. It may be argued that the coal mines are protected by the existing duty. This was referred to by an hon. member this afternoon. But the import duty on coal is really not protective, for this reason, that the coals from the state of Washington belong to a comparatively recent geological period. It is an inferior class of coal, and there is no demand for it in British Columbia. It is only in cases like strikes or labour troubles that the coal from the state of Washington is shipped, into British Columbia, and, of course, it then pays a duty of 53 cents a ton. I claim that the 53 cents is of no real practical benefit or protection to the coal mining industry of the island. There is another thing which probably the imposition of this duty will accomplish, and I commend this to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark). This duty should give an impetus to exploration for oil fields in the western provinces, and if it accomplished that I think it would be worth while imposing the duty. I understand that the prospects of oil in Alberta and the northwestern provinces are very good, indeed, and I have no doubt the day will come when oil will be found in sufficient quantities to be commercially valuable, and, perhaps, the question of duties then might be reconsidered. If oil was produced in Canada in sufficient quantities, so that we would have no fear of the invasion of foreign fuel oil, then the question of this duty could be reconsidered-But I do maintain that a duty on fuel oil at this particular time should give a stimulus to oil exploration in the northwestern provinces. In conclusion, I submit that this duty will fill the two-fold purpose of giving a good revenue to the Government at a time when it is needed, aqd protecting an industry which, should ihe invasion of fuel oil continue in the same ratio as it has in the past, would be threatened with extinction.
Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM: This seems to be a very hard country to govern, and the people seem to be very difficult people to please. Most of the day one section of the country has been asking for a duty to encourage the production of apples, while another section of Canada has been opposing it because it will tend to make the apples too dear. We find to-night the Minister of Finance and my hon. friend who has just sat down approaching this subject of a duty on fuel' oil from different angles altogether. Of course the Minister of Fin ance admitted casually that it might help the coal industry, but if it helps the coal business it will not help him, because the moment the coal takes the place of fuel oil, the revenue which the Minister of Finance is after ceases. Both of these objects cannot be attained except in the happy way the hon. member from Nanaimo suggests, that the Minister of Finance can have whatever revenue he can get from the present duties, but cannot get any more. There is a difference between Ontario and British Columbia. Only last week the province of Ontario paid over $8,000,000 for the purpose of getting cheap power, while British Columbia is asking for legislation to prevent the obtaining of cheap power. It is most difficult for legislators to know just what to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The British Columbia
coal industry is a great industry. Any person who knows anything about it can sympathize fully with the position of the hon. member for Nanaimo. Once deprive that portion of the province of this industry and you injure it very materially. On the other hand, I think it is going to be absolutely impossible to suppress the more extensive use of oil as a fuel. It is admitted that it is cheaper. My hon. friend is asking the imposition of the duty; but fuel oil is so much cheaper that people are using it in place of coal. It is a serious situation so far as coal is concerned, but I am inclined to think that some other way out of the difficulty will have to be found because, to my mind, fuel oil is going to be used more and more. In this province electricity is becoming the chief motive power and under a provincial arrangement through the Hydro-Electric (Commission, this power is being distributed all over Ontario for the use of manufacturers, and is even being carried into the homes of the farmers and small consumers at very reasonable rates. This is necessary. The manufacturers of Ontario find it necessary in order to compete with the cheap power across the line, where coal is produced in abundance and where they have cheap electric power as well. If that be the case, no argument can be advanced in favour of increasing the cost of power to men engaged either in transportation or any other business requiring cheap power, if

we are to make Canada a country capable of producing in competition with other countries.
Even the small consumer of power in his own home, or on his farm, gets the advantage of this cheap power. I suppose my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Shepherd) knows that the Imperial Oil Company has recently established a plant in the West for the sole purpose of being close to their customers, and,- I presume, of supplying this fuel oil at an even cheaper price than it has been supplied at hitherto. I am told that the company expects to do that.
That is not the oil to which I refer. That was explained by the minister. The oil used on the prairies is heavy distillates. The Imperial Oil Company are not distributing fuel oil.

They may be distributing the refined article, but I should think they will distribute fuel oil as well when they get properly in motion. At least, I am told it 'is one of their objects, to bring that fuel closer to the market. It is a difficult problem. While I sympathize to the fullest extent with the wish of those who are rightly interested in the coal industry, I think they will have to be prepared in the future, and before very long, to see oil used as fuel to a very large extent. The Board of Railway Commissioners may insist that all the railway companies shall use oil as fuel. I am not sure, but I think recommendations have been made to them in the past with that object in view, in order to protect the forests of British Columbia from fire, which causes great havoc. Already two of the great transcontinental lines, the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk Pacific, are using oil as fuel. The Canadian Northern railway is not using oil as fuel because that company have some interest in extensive coal mines, and, of course, have their own coal.
I may assure my hon. friend that the Canadian Northern do not own the Canadian Collieries.
They own other coal deposits, if not the Canadian Collieries. At any rate, I know that several charters were got to enable them to run to their coal mines in British Columbia.

The Canadian Northern Company, or rather Sir William Mackenzie, 
floated a company which took >ver the Dunsmuir colliery. That is the only mine in which, I think, they are interested in in British Columbia, and they are not interested' in that to anv great extent. That was a personal speculation of Sir William Mackenzie's, and he has turned it over to British investors, and has practically no interest in it now.

I was not criticising them it all; I was simply pointing out that the two railway companies which have no interest in coal mines use oil. and that if it is found to be beneficial the Board o( Rail-Aray Commissioners may make an order to the Canadian Northern to do the same thing. The two railway companies which are using oil are not acting on an order from the Railway Cbmmission. After all, I am inclined to think that this duty will not help the coal industry so much as it will help to get revenue for the Finance Minister. I sympathize with my hon. friend from Nanaimo, but I do not think it will have the effect of stopping the use of fuel oil, because I think that fuel oil will be cheaper in the years to come than it is now and that there will be better facilities for using it, and better means of getting it. It will be apt to become cheaper instead of dearer. Those who use it tell me that it is superior to coal as a fuel, for the purposes to which it is put. I am rather inclined to think that the Minister of Finance will get considerable revenue out of the transportation companies. It may be regrettable that the one transportation company, out of which he expects to get his war tax, is one which my hon. friend from Nanaimo says will contribute the greatest amount of revenue from this new tax.

I want to congratulate the hon member from Nanaimo upon his perfect frankness, and upon the manner in which he has presented his case this evening. From the statements made by the hon. member it appears that this tax has been imposed at the request of the hon. member from Nanaimo, and probably of other gentlemen from his province. It also seems perfectly plain that it is proposed with the object of preventing the consumption of fuel oil, and, to that extent, of assisting or encouraging the consumption of coal. If that is the object, it means that the minister will not get revenue out of it so much as that the people who have

to use .power in British Columbia will pay a greater price for their fuel. If the people of British Columbia are satisfied with that arrangement, and if the transportation companies are satisfied with it, possibly no very great harm may accrue, because we can all appreciate the importance of keeping the coal mines in British Columbia going. But the difficulty I see is that people in other parts of the country, who are not so much interested in keeping the coal mines of British Columbia operating, are going to suffer as well. I think the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Nanaimo ' will see the force of that argument. If you are going to make power expensive, you are going, just to that extent, to increase the expense of production, of business, of manufacture, and of transportation, and to affect practically every phase of industrial life in Canada. That is the principle involved, it seems to me; that is the almost vicious side of it.
My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) referred to the province of Ontario. That province probably offers a ground of comparison to some extent, but it is not a good comparison, because in Ontario, unfortunately, they have no coal. But go further east, go down to the Maritime Provinces, where we have both coal and water-powers. What would be thought if the people of the Maritime Provinces and Quebec came to Parliament and asked that a heavy embargo be placed upon the production of water-power? Would you not say that either they were crazy or selfish, or that something was wrong with their mental operations? Yet I do not see any difference between that proposition and the proposition put forward by the hon. gentlemen from British Columbia, who frankly say: It is true we want to make power dearer, but we want to do so in order to help the coal mines of British Columbia. Go down, if you will, to the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, or to Eastern Quebec, where Nova Scotia and New Brunswick coal is used practically exclusively; if this Parliament were to say: We are going to put, a tax oil your horsepower or unit; your water-power is too cheap, so cheap that it is taking the place of coal, therefore we ought to do something in order to prevent you from using this cheap power and in order to develop the coal mines-I do not know what the people of British Columbia would say to a proposition of that kind, but I know what would happen down east. Any man who
made such a proposition would meet with a very warm reception.
Water-power is a home product, but fuel oil is not.

It is partly, but I do not think that that helps my hon. friend much. The effect would be the same as on the coal industry. I do think that this is class legislation, that it is legislation intended evidently-indeed, the thing is admitted frankly-to help put a certain industry in one portion of Canada to the detriment of dozens and dozens of other industries in other portions of Canada. If my hon. friend feels like pressing it through, I presume it will go through, but I want to register my protest against the principle involved,. I believe the hon. member for Nanaimo knows a little more of what he is talking about than does the minister. I do not say that offensively, but I wish it to be understood as being complimentary' to the hon. member for Nanaimo. I believe the member for Nanaimo is right when he says that the result of this legislation will be an increased consumption of coal and a stoppage of the importation of fuel oil, with the result that we will have protection in its most vicious form, and the revenue will not be bene-fitted to any extent thereby. If this were put forward purely as a revenue producer at a time when the country needs revenue and we must have revenue from some source, we would all have to bury our principles and, our ideas upon many things. The Minister of Finance says this is a revenue measure, but if we are to take the evidence of the gentleman who knows all about it, we must come to the conclusion that this is not a revenue producer, but a protective policy pure and simple in order to boost the production of coal in British Columbia, and to make the cost of land and marine transportation, and the heating of houses, very much higher in Canada in the future than it has been in the past.
I would like to ask the hon. member for Nanaimo if fuel oil is used in the heating of houses in British Columbia to any extent, or is it confined, to the larger office buildings and hotels?
Just to the larger buildings, sky scrapers, and very few of them.

The impression is prevalent that the Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian Pacific are using oil in the moun-

tains as the result of the exercise of authority either by this Government directly, or by the Railway Commission. I would like . to ask the minister if there is any warrant for the assumption that they have not been free agents in the matter of the adoption of oil instead of coal burning locomotives?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I made inquiry, and I was informed that there is no warrant for such an assertion. There appears to have been no order made on the subject either by the Government or by the Railway Commission.

Did my hon. friend's inquiries go far enough to find out whether such an order had been made by the Government of British Columbia? I understand that oil burning engines were adopted in the interest of forest protection and I find it hard to believe that both of these companies would introduce oil burning engines at great expense unless they were compelled to do so. Would my hon. friend tell the committee if the Government of British Columbia exercised that authority?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that no such authority was exercised by the Government of British Columbia, but a request [DOT] might have been made by the Forestry Branch of that province. I understand that no order has been made. It would appear to me, from the consideration I have given the matter, that the railway companies will continue to make use of fuel oil. It is true they will have to pay this additional duty upon it, but it would not appear to me that the amount which they would be called upon to pay is unreasonable, having regard to the fact that we are in need of revenue-
That is not the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -and that this fuel oil has been on the free list. It is the point in so far as the question put to me by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) is concerned. Let me ask my hon. friend from Nova Scotia (Mr. Maclean) a question. He is aware that there is a duty upon coal. I do not know a more important subject, from the tariff standpoint, than the duty upon coal in so far as Nova Scotia is concerned. I do not believe any gentleman from Nova Scotia would advocate taking that duty off.
That is not this case at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is this case to a certain extent.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why is the duty on coal valued by Nova Scotia? Because it is a protection given to the coal industry of that province.

In the market outside
of the province itself. It is not designed as a protection within the province which is producing the coal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend say that the only purpose served by the duty on coal in so far as Nova Scotia is concerned is in respect to the export business?

From the province to
other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, this is Canada. It is true we have different, provinces. But would my hon. friend say that coal would sell as high in Montreal, or in Ontario, if there was no duty on coal?
My hon. friend says that the increase in the duty on apples will not make any difference in the price. If that is so it should not make any difference in the price of coal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What is the position of the coal mining industry of British Columbia? I thought the statement of my hon. friend from Nanaimo was a reasonably fair statement. He said that this would not prevent the use of fuel oil but that it would tend to put fuel oil and coal upon a parity. He made one or two points of extreme weight. One was that the competition at present is not fair. The coal mining industry of British Columbia pays a royalty to the British Columbia Government. The coal mining industry of British Columbia supports several thousand workmen and their families and plays a very important part in the economy of the entire province. On the other hand, what Canadian labour is employed in so far as fuel oil is concerned? What part does its production play in the economy of British Columbia? What royalty does it pay in which the province of British Columbia is in any way a participator? Is it quite fair that there should be a protective duty which prevents American coal from entering into competition with Nova Scotia coal, in the interest of the coal operatives of Nova Scotia and I am entirely in favour of

that tariff-and that the coal mining industry of British Columbia, equally important, relatively, to that province, should have no measure of protection against the competition described by the hon. member for Nanaimo??
Mr. A. K. M4CLEAN: They have the duty on coal.
They have the same protection that the Nova Scotia coal miners have.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no coal imported into British Columbia.

Nor into Nova Scotia
either.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should think not into
Nova Scotia. But there is no foreign coal imported into British Columbia. It's geographical situation is different from the geographical situation of the East. The effect of this tariff is going to be precisely what I have said. I say perfectly frankly, as I said at the beginning that it will give a large revenue and that incidentally it will give a measure of protection to the coal mining industry of British Columbia. Has my hon. friend ever heard of a tariff policy for revenue and incidental protection? Has he ever heard that expression before? I think he has. There is nothing strange about this proposition at all. It will give the Dominion Government a substantial revenue and it is not going to prevent the use of fuel oil. It certainly will not in the province of Ontario and it certainly will not in the province of British Columbia, but it will have a tendency towards bringing about a greater use proportionately of coal and consequently it will inure to the advantage of the British Columbia coal industry just as the tariff on coal inures to the advantage of the Nova Scotia coal industry, as it should.

If the resolution passes now I suppose we can discuss these patters further when the Bill is 'brought down. This duty upon fuel oil opens a much bigger question than I think the members of the committee thought of. The tariff item was not explained at all by the minister in his Budget speech, and attention had not been directed to it specifically by anybody in this House until this evening. From the standpoint of British Columbia, it may be very undesirable to impose this duty; I do not say that it is, I do not pretend to know the subject very well.
The minister has referred to certain oils mentioned or alluded to in this item. Is gasolene subject to this duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Gasolene is not
affected in any way by the tariff changes proposed in the Budget.
What are the oils, calling them by their commercial names, which are affected?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Fuel oil, and the other oils known as heavy distillates, such as gas oil, road oil, and petroleum tailings. These latter three are known under the comprehensive name of heavy distillates. The heavy distillates are used in what are known as internal combustion traction engines, which are largely used in the West.
I am sorry to say I cannot agree. Gasolene is what is used in these traction engines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Gasolene is also used. I am informed that about 1,000,000 gallons of the heavy distillates are used. The duty on these heavy distillates has been reduced from 2J cents to half a cent a gallon. That is a very substantial reduction upon about a million gallons of oil.

That is the point I want to get at. Upon what quantity is the reduction madp? My impression is that the minister has entirely over-stated the amount, because I am satisfied that a very large proportion of the traction power in the West is gasolene.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I may say that gasolene is free, except for the war tax.
Resolution reported.	,
On motion of Sir Thomas White, the House adjourned at 11.03 p.m.
Thursday, March 16, 1916.
